tamil:
வீழ்வாரின் இன்சொல் பெறாஅது உலகத்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
transliteration:
Veezhvaarin insol peraaadhu ulakaththu
vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
current_meaning: No one in the world is as hard-hearted, or as brave, as a woman who keeps on living without even one kind word from the one she loves.
elementary: Imagine waiting every day for a letter from someone you love, and none ever comes, yet you keep getting up and going to school. That takes a very strong heart. The Kural says it is almost too strong.
university: Vaṉkaṇār means both ‘the hard-hearted, cruel’ and ‘the brave, enduring’, and the couplet exploits the ambiguity with self-irony: the heroine says that those who go on living in the world (ulakattu vāḻvār) without receiving (peṟāatu) even a sweet word (iṉcol) from their beloved (vīḻvār) are the most vaṉkaṇ of all. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read vaṉkaṇmai as the stony endurance of separation; Pappaiah’s ‘no one is more cruel’ and Kalaignar’s ‘no one has so stony a heart’ stress self-reproach, while Pope chooses the heroic sense: ‘Who hear from lover’s lips no pleasant word from day to day, / Yet in the world live out their life,- no braver souls than they!’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நசைஇயார் நல்கார் எனினும் அவர்மாட்டு
இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு.
transliteration:
Nasai-iyaar nalkaar eninum avarmaattu
isaiyum iniya sevikku.
current_meaning: Even if the one I long for shows me no kindness, every word about him, even his name, is still sweet to my ears.
elementary: Sometimes when you miss someone, just hearing their name makes you smile, even if they haven’t called you. The girl in this couplet feels that way: anything about him sounds like music.
university: Nacaiiyār (with alapeṭai) is ‘the one longed for’; nalkār eṉiṉum, ‘even though he grants no grace’; avar māṭṭu icaiyum, ‘even what is heard of / from him’, is iṉiya cevikku, ‘sweet to the ear.’ The word icai is read two ways: as ‘fame, praise’ (Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar: hearing others praise him is honey to her), or as ‘word, sound’ (Pappaiah: any word from him is sweet). Pope follows the second: ‘Though he my heart desires no grace accords to me, / Yet every accent of his voice is melody.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய் கடலைச்
செறாஅஅய் வாழிய நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Uraaarkku urunoi uraippaai kadalaich
cheraaaai vaazhiya nenju.
current_meaning: Bless you, my heart! Telling your great pain to someone who does not care about you is like trying to fill up the sea.
elementary: Imagine trying to fill the ocean with a bucket. No matter how much you pour, it never fills. The girl tells her own heart that telling her sadness to someone who doesn’t care is just like that.
university: The chapter closes with an apostrophe to the heart (neñcu), a figure that the next chapters develop. Uṟāarkku is ‘to one who is not attached (to you)’, uṟunōy ‘the great affliction (you suffer)’, uraippāy ‘you who tell’; kaṭalaic ceṟāaay is read as an ironic imperative, ‘(go and) fill up the sea!’ Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar, is comparative: filling the sea would be easier than winning comfort from the indifferent. Vāḻiya, ‘may you live / bless you’, is half-pitying, half-mocking. Pope: ‘Tell him thy pain that loves not thee? / Farewell, my soul, fill up the sea!’, while his prose gloss reads the sea as her own sea of sorrow. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both with the triple alapeṭai செறாஅஅய்.

tamil:
உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ் செய்தலால்
கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது.
transliteration:
Ullinum theeraap perumakizh seydhalaal
kallinum kaamam inidhu.
current_meaning: Love is sweeter than strong drink. Drink makes you happy only while you drink it, but love gives great joy that never runs out, even when you only remember it.
elementary: A sweet drink makes you happy only while you are sipping it. But think of a wonderful day with someone you love, and you smile all over again. That is why the poet says love is sweeter than any drink: even the memory of it makes you glad.
university: Chapter 121, ninaintavar pulampal (‘the lament of those who remember’), stands in the karpiyal (wedded love) sequence on separation, where the absent partner is sustained and tormented by memory. The opening couplet sets the chapter’s premise by comparison with kaḷ (toddy, palm wine): uḷḷiṉum, ‘even when merely thought of’, love yields tīrā perumakiḻ, a great joy that does not run out, whereas kaḷ delights only when consumed, as Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss. Solomon Pappaiah, following the traditional assignment, hears the husband speaking of past union with his wife, while modern readers often extend it to both lovers. Pope renders: ‘From thought of her unfailing gladness springs, / Sweeter than palm-rice wine the joy love brings.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எனைத்தொன்று இனிதேகாண் காமம்தாம் வீழ்வார்
நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல்.
transliteration:
Enaiththondru inidhekaan kaamamdhaam veezhvaar
ninaippa varuvadhondru il.
current_meaning: Love is sweet in every way. When you think of the one you love, no pain of being apart comes to you.
elementary: When your best friend moves away, you miss them. But when you think about the funny games you played together, the sad feeling goes away for a while. The poet says love is like that: just thinking of the person you love can chase the sadness off.
university: The couplet explains why love is sweet ‘in every way’ (eṉaittoṉṟu): to think of those one desires (tām vīḻvār) brings no suffering (varuvatu oṉṟu il), so love delights both in union and in separation; Parimelazhagar, who treats it as a continuation of the previous couplet’s speaker, says Valluvar called it sweet ‘in any measure’ because it is equally sweet when lovers are together and apart. Manakkudavar and Parip Perumal instead make it the heroine’s rejoinder to a confidante who warns that her pining will harm her. There is a genuine textual variant: Perundevanar, commenting on the Virasoliyam, quotes the second line as niṉaikka varuvatu oṉṟu uṇṭu (‘there is something that comes when one thinks’), whereas Parimelazhagar reads niṉaippa varuvatu oṉṟu il, the standard text (as given on kuralthiran.com). Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the head-word with typographical slips (eṉaittoṉaṟu, and ēl for il), which are corrected here against kuralthiran.com and the commentaries’ glosses.

tamil:
நினைப்பவர் போன்று நினையார்கொல் தும்மல்
சினைப்பது போன்று கெடும்.
transliteration:
Ninaippavar poandru ninaiyaarkol thummal
sinaippadhu poandru kedum.
current_meaning: I felt a sneeze coming, which people say means someone far away is thinking of you, but it faded. Did he start to think of me and then stop?
elementary: Some people say that if you sneeze, someone far away is thinking of you. The lady in this poem feels a sneeze coming, and then it goes away! She worries: did he start to think of me and then stop? It is a gentle, funny way to show how much she wants to be remembered.
university: The image rests on the folk belief, presupposed by all the glosses, that a sneeze signals that someone far away is thinking of one. The heroine feels a sneeze ‘budding’ (ciṉaippatu, from ciṉai, to sprout) and then subsiding (keṭum), and asks whether her husband, seeming to think of her, has stopped (niṉaippavar pōṉṟu niṉaiyār-kol). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all render it this way, and Pope gives: ‘A fit of sneezing threatened, but it passed away; / He seemed to think of me, but do his fancies stray?’ The couplet’s comedy is tender: a trivial bodily flicker becomes evidence in a lover’s anxious inquiry. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து எந்நெஞ்சத்து
ஓஒ உளரே அவர்.
transliteration:
Yaamum ulaengol avarnenjaththu ennenjaththu
oo-o ulare avar.
current_meaning: Do I have a place in his heart too? Oh, he lives in my heart all the time.
elementary: Imagine you think about your grandma every single day while she is far away. You might wonder, ‘Does Grandma think about me too?’ The lady in this poem asks the same: he is always in my heart, but am I in his?
university: The couplet sets two hearts side by side: avar neñcattu (‘in his heart’) and en neñcattu (‘in my heart’). The exclamation ōo (lengthened ō, ‘alas’ or ‘oh!’) marks her certainty that he is unceasingly present in her own heart (uḷarē avar), while the particle kol turns her own presence in his heart into an anxious question (yāmum uḷēṅ-kol). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘do we too remain without leaving in his heart?’, and Pope renders: ‘Have I a place within his heart? / From mine, alas! he never doth depart.’ The royal plural yām is the heroine’s usual self-reference in the Kamattuppal. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார் நாணார்கொல்
எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்.
transliteration:
Thamnenjaththu emmaik katikondaar naanaarkol
emnenjaththu ovaa varal.
current_meaning: He keeps me out of his own heart. Is he not ashamed to keep coming into mine again and again, without a break?
elementary: Imagine a friend who never lets you into their clubhouse, but keeps walking into yours whenever they like! The lady in this poem jokes that her husband does that with hearts: he keeps visiting her thoughts all day, but she wonders if he lets her into his.
university: The couplet turns the previous question into a playful accusation. Kaṭi koṇṭār means ‘those who have set a guard against’ (kaṭi, ‘watch, prohibition’): Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘he who has kept guard in his heart so that we may not enter’, and Pope renders ‘Me from his heart he jealously excludes: / Hath he no shame who ceaseless on my heart intrudes?’ Ōvā varal is ‘coming without ceasing’, and nāṇār-kol asks ‘is he not ashamed?’, invoking nāṇ, the sense of shame and propriety prized in the Kural. The reproach is affectionate: his constant ‘visits’ are simply her inability to stop thinking of him. One modern gloss (Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh.com) reads kaṭi as ‘scold’, but the guarding sense is standard. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மற்றியான் என்னுளேன் மன்னோ அவரொடியான்
உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்.
transliteration:
Matriyaan ennulen manno avarodiyaan
utranaal ulla ulen.
current_meaning: What else keeps me alive? I live only by remembering the happy days I spent with him.
elementary: When someone you love is far away, you might look at photos of happy times together to feel better. The lady in this poem says remembering their happy days is what keeps her going, like food that keeps her strong.
university: The couplet makes memory the very means of survival. Avaroṭu yāṉ uṟṟa nāḷ are ‘the days when I was joined with him’; uḷḷa, ‘by recalling’, I live (uḷēṉ). The first line’s maṟṟu yāṉ eṉṉ uḷēṉ, ‘otherwise, by what do I live?’, carries the particles maṉ and ō, which the commentators treat as expletives adding pathos. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss: ‘It is by thinking of the days I was with him that I am alive; by what else?’ Pope renders: ‘How live I yet? I live to ponder o’er / The days of bliss with him that are no more.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மறப்பின் எவனாவன் மற்கொல் மறப்பறியேன்
உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Marappin evanaavan markol marappariyaen
ullinum ullam sudum.
current_meaning: What would happen to me if I ever forgot him? I never forget him, and even remembering him burns my heart.
elementary: Missing someone can hurt a little, like a warm ache inside. But the lady in this poem says that forgetting him would be even worse, because the memories are part of who she is. So she keeps remembering, even though it stings.
university: The couplet balances two pains. Maṟappu aṟiyēṉ, ‘I know no forgetting’, yet even recalling (uḷḷiṉum) burns the heart (uḷḷam cuṭum), with a characteristic pun on uḷḷu (‘to think’) and uḷḷam (‘heart, mind’); what then would I become if I forgot (maṟappiṉ evaṉ āvaṉ)? Maṟ-kol combines the particles maṉ and kol. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as ‘even remembering without forgetting, the pain of separation burns; if I forgot, how could I live?’, while Puliyur Kesikan (on thirukkural.net) reads ‘if I even think of forgetting, that thought burns’. Pope renders: ‘If I remembered not what were I then? And yet, / The fiery smart of what my spirit knows not to forget!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார் அனைத்தன்றோ
காதலர் செய்யும் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Enaiththu ninaippinum kaayaar anaiththandroa
kaadhalar seyyum sirappu.
current_meaning: However much I think of him, he never gets angry with me for it. Isn't that the great kindness my loved one shows me?
elementary: Some people get grumpy if you call them too many times. But the lady in this poem says that no matter how often she thinks about her husband, he never gets cross about it. She feels that is his special gift to her.
university: The heroine finds consolation in a small, wry point: however much (eṉaittu) she thinks of him, he does not grow angry (kāyār, from kāy, ‘to be angry, to burn’). Aṉaittu aṉṟō, ‘is it not that much?’, makes this the measure of the ciṟappu, the special honour or favour her beloved bestows. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render ciṟappu as ‘great help’ (uṭavi), Solomon Pappaiah as ‘the joy he gives’, and Pope as ‘This honour doth my love on me bestow.’ The humour is gentle: he cannot object to what he cannot see, so her freedom to remember is the one gift his absence still allows. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
விளியுமென் இன்னுயிர் வேறல்லம் என்பார்
அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து.
transliteration:
Viliyumen innuyir vaerallam enpaar
aliyinmai aatra ninaindhu.
current_meaning: My dear life is slipping away as I keep thinking how unkind he is now, the one who used to say, "We two are not separate."
elementary: Imagine a best friend who always said, ‘We are like twins, we will never be apart,’ and then went away. You might feel very sad remembering those words. The lady in this poem feels like that, and the memory makes her heart ache.
university: The couplet sets the husband’s past words against his present conduct. Vēṟu allam, ‘we are not different’, is his former vow of oneness (Kalaignar: ‘we are one, not two’); aḷiyiṉmai, ‘lack of tender grace’ (aḷi, ‘kindness, compassion’), is how she now reads his absence. Thinking on it too much (āṟṟa niṉaintu), her ‘sweet life’ (iṉṉuyir) is perishing (viḷiyum). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress the contrast between what he ‘used to say’ and his present want of love, and Pope renders: ‘Dear life departs, when his ungracious deeds I ponder o’er, / Who said erewhile, “We’re one for evermore.”’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
விடாஅது சென்றாரைக் கண்ணினால் காணப்
படாஅதி வாழி மதி.
transliteration:
Vitaaadhu sendraaraik kanninaal kaanap
pataaadhi vaazhi madhi.
current_meaning: Long live you, Moon! Please do not set, so my eyes can find him, the one who went away but never left my heart.
elementary: When someone you love is far away, you might look up at the moon and think, ‘They can see the moon too!’ The lady in this poem asks the moon not to go down, so that she can keep looking, as if the moon could help her find him.
university: The heroine addresses the moon (mati) with a blessing (vāḻi, ‘may you live long’) and a plea: paṭāa-ti, ‘do not set’ (paṭu, ‘to go down, set’), so that she may see with her eyes (kaṇṇiṉāl kāṇa) him who left without leaving (viṭāatu ceṉṟār), that is, who went away but never left her heart. Parimelazhagar’s celebrated gloss explains that since the moon is looked at by both lovers, their eyes meet in it, so she ‘sees’ him at least by the measure of the eye. Manakkudavar and Parip Perumal read paṭāatu (‘the moon does not set’) and take it as a complaint: if the moon set, she could sleep and meet him in dreams; Parimelazhagar notes this reading and its sense. Kalingar is reported to have placed this couplet in chapter 127 (avarvayiṉ vitumpal) instead (all as summarised on kuralthiran.com). Pope renders: ‘Set not; so may’st thou prosper, moon! that eyes may see / My love who went away, but ever bides with me.’ The standard text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காதலர் தூதொடு வந்த கனவினுக்கு
யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து.
transliteration:
Kaadhalar thoodhodu vandha kanavinukku
yaadhusey vaenkol virundhu.
current_meaning: A dream came to me carrying a message from my faraway love. What special meal can I give that dream, like a guest, to thank it?
elementary: Imagine you are missing a grandparent who lives far away, and one night you dream they send you a happy note saying they will visit soon. You wake up so glad that you want to thank the dream itself, as if it were a postman who knocked at your door with the best letter ever.
university: Chapter 122, kaṉavunilai uraittal (‘telling of the state of dreams’), continues the karpiyal sequence on separation: in the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the wife, long parted from her husband, tells her confidante (tōḻi) what she has seen in dreams, and the dreams become her way of enduring absence. The opening couplet personifies the dream as a guest who arrives with a tūtu (messenger, embassy), so that the hospitality word viruntu (feast offered to a guest, the virtue praised in Aṟam ch. 9) is turned on the dream itself; yātu ceyvēṉ-kol is a helpless rhetorical question, ‘what can I possibly do?’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss the line as asking what return (kaimmāṟu) she can make to the dream that came with her lover’s envoy. Pope renders: ‘It came and brought to me, that nightly vision rare, / A message from my love,- what feast shall I prepare?’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (which spells the chapter title as two words, kaṉavunilai uraittal).

tamil:
கயலுண்கண் யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சிற் கலந்தார்க்கு
உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன் மன்.
transliteration:
Kayalunkan yaanirappath thunjir kalandhaarkku
uyalunmai saatruvaen man.
current_meaning: If my fish-shaped eyes would only fall asleep when I beg them, I could tell my love, when he comes in my dream, how hard it has been to stay alive.
elementary: Have you ever had so much to tell someone that you lay awake and couldn’t sleep? This girl wants to fall asleep so she can meet her faraway husband in a dream and tell him how hard it has been, but the worry keeps her eyes wide open.
university: Kayal uṇ kaṇ, ‘carp-like eyes lined with collyrium’, is a stock Sangam image of feminine beauty, here made pathetic: the eyes that once drew the lover now refuse the sleep (tuñcil, ‘if they sleep’) that would let her meet him. Yāṉ irappa means ‘as I beg’, casting the heroine as a supplicant to her own eyes. Kalantārkku, ‘to him who united with me’, names the husband by their past union; uyal uṇmai is ‘the truth of my survival’, i.e. how she has scraped through the separation, and cāṟṟuvēṉ ‘I would declare’. The closing particle maṉ marks a wish that cannot be fulfilled, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan render as ‘I would tell him, if only’. Pope: ‘If my dark, carp-like eye will close in sleep, as I implore, / The tale of my long-suffering life I’ll tell my loved one o’er.’ Both base sources print the same text.

tamil:
நனவினால் நல்கா தவரைக் கனவினால்
காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaa thavaraik kanavinaal
kaantalin unten uyir.
current_meaning: He is not kind to me while I am awake. But I see him in my dreams, and that is what keeps me alive.
elementary: Think of a plant on a windowsill that only gets a little sunlight each morning. It is just enough to keep it alive. For this woman, seeing her husband in dreams is that little bit of sunlight that keeps her going until he comes home.
university: The couplet sets up the chapter’s governing antithesis of naṉavu (waking) and kaṉavu (dream), each in the instrumental (naṉaviṉāl, kaṉaviṉāl, ‘by waking’, ‘by dream’). Nalkātavar, ‘he who does not grant grace’, from nalku (to show favour, bestow love), names the absent husband by his failure to come; the word recurs through the chapter (1214, 1217, 1219) and functions almost as an epithet. Kāṇṭaliṉ, ‘because of seeing’, gives the cause, and uṇṭu eṉ uyir, ‘my life exists’, makes the dream the slender thread on which her life hangs. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as ‘my life has not yet left me only because I see him in dreams’. Pope: ‘Him, who in waking hour no kindness shows, / In dreams I see; and so my lifetime goes!’ The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
கனவினான் உண்டாகும் காமம் நனவினான்
நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு.
transliteration:
Kanavinaan undaakum kaamam nanavinaan
nalkaarai naatith thararku.
current_meaning: Love's joy comes to me in my dreams, because the dream goes looking for the one who is not kind to me when I am awake, and brings him to me.
elementary: Imagine a friendly dog that runs off every night and comes back pulling your best friend by the sleeve so you can play together. Here the dream is like that helpful dog: it goes and finds the husband who is far away and brings him home, just for the night.
university: Here the dream is not merely a place but an agent: nāṭi, ‘having searched out’, and taraṟku, ‘in order to give, bring’, make it a go-between who fetches the reluctant lover. The forms kaṉaviṉāṉ and naṉaviṉāṉ use the older instrumental ending -āṉ for -āl, a metrical variant noted in Tamil grammatical tradition. Kāmam here is the pleasure of love, not mere desire; nalkārai repeats the epithet ‘him who grants no grace’ from 1213. Varadarasanar reads the couplet as ‘love-incidents arise in dreams in order to seek out and bring the lover’, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar shift the stress to the joy the dream gives by bringing him. Pope: ‘Some pleasure I enjoy when him who loves not me / In waking hours, the vision searches out and makes me see.’ Text identical on both sites.

tamil:
நனவினால் கண்டதூஉம் ஆங்கே கனவுந்தான்
கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal kandadhooum aange kanavundhaan
kanda pozhudhae inidhu.
current_meaning: Seeing him while I was awake was sweet only while it lasted. Seeing him in a dream is just the same, sweet for the moment I see him.
elementary: An ice-cream cone is lovely while you are eating it, and then it’s gone. A dream about someone you love is the same: it is just as lovely while it lasts. This woman says both kinds of seeing, awake and dreaming, are sweet, but only in the moment.
university: Kaṇṭatūum is kaṇṭatu, ‘what was seen’, with uyir-aḷapeṭai, the metrical prolongation of the vowel (-ūum) that Tamil prosody uses to fill out a foot. Āṅkē, ‘just then, at that time’, and kaṇṭa poḻutē, ‘at the very moment of seeing’, set the two experiences on a level: both sweetnesses are bounded by the moment. Varadarasanar stresses the limitation (‘only at that time… only at the time it is seen’), whereas Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress the equality (‘both were pleasures to me’); the couplet can carry both, a consolation tinged with the knowledge that waking joy too was fleeting. Pope: ‘As what I then beheld in waking hour was sweet, / So pleasant dreams in hour of sleep my spirit greet.’ Both base sources print the same text.

tamil:
நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின் கனவினால்
காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்.
transliteration:
Nanavena ondrillai aayin kanavinaal
kaadhalar neengalar man.
current_meaning: If there were no such thing as being awake, my love, who comes to me in dreams, would never leave me.
elementary: Have you ever had a really happy dream and felt sad when the alarm clock rang? This woman wishes there were no alarm clock at all, no waking up, so that the husband she sees in her dreams could stay with her forever.
university: Naṉavu eṉa oṉṟu illai āyiṉ, ‘if there were no one thing called waking’, is a bold counterfactual that makes waking itself the villain; Pappaiah even calls it ‘a cruel sinner’ (koṭiya pāvi), and Kalaignar has it ‘suddenly coming to spoil’ the meeting. Nīṅkalar, ‘he would not depart’, describes the lover in the dream, and the final particle maṉ again marks an impossible wish, as in 1212. The couplet inverts the common wisdom that dreams are unreal and waking true: for the heroine, waking is what takes the beloved away. Pope: ‘And if there were no waking hour, my love / In dreams would never from my side remove.’ Text identical on both sites.

tamil:
நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார் கனவனால்
என்எம்மைப் பீழிப் பது.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaak kotiyaar kanavanaal
en-emmaip peezhip padhu.
current_meaning: He is cruel and not kind to me when I am awake. So why does he come into my dreams only to hurt me?
elementary: Imagine a friend who never answers your calls in the daytime but keeps popping up in your dreams. You might grumble, ‘If you won’t come and play when I’m awake, why do you keep visiting me at night and making me miss you even more?’
university: The mood turns from gratitude to reproach. Koṭiyār, ‘the cruel one’ (honorific plural), is a lover’s accusation, and pīḻippatu, ‘tormenting’, from pīḻ (to afflict, squeeze), names the pain of a dream that teases without fulfilling. Eṉ is the interrogative ‘why’, and emmai the plural ‘us’, the heroine speaking of herself with the inclusive dignity common in akam speech. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print kaṉavaṉāl in the first line, where many editions have the regular instrumental kaṉaviṉāl; the sense is unaffected. Kalaignar glosses the torment as the dream ‘enlarging the grief of separation’. Pope: ‘The cruel one, in waking hour, who all ungracious seems, / Why should he thus torment my soul in nightly dreams?’

tamil:
துஞ்சுங்கால் தோள்மேலர் ஆகி விழிக்குங்கால்
நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து.
transliteration:
Thunjungaal thoalmelar aaki vizhikkungaal
nenjaththar aavar viraindhu.
current_meaning: When I sleep, he rests on my shoulders. The moment I wake up, he quickly slips back into my heart.
elementary: Think of a kitten that naps on your shoulder, and when you sit up it darts inside your jacket to stay warm. The husband in this poem is like that: in sleep he is right beside her, and when she wakes up he hurries to hide in her heart, so he is never really gone.
university: This is the chapter’s most celebrated couplet for its grace. Tuñcuṅkāl / viḻikkuṅkāl (‘when I sleep’ / ‘when I wake’) frame a perfect parallel, and tōḷmēlar (‘he who is on my shoulders’) answers neñcattar (‘he who is in my heart’), so that the beloved merely changes residence and is never absent. Viraintu, ‘swiftly’, gives the image a playful quickness, as if he darts inward at the first stir of waking. Pappaiah reads it as ‘my lord, who always lives in my heart, lies on my shoulder when I sleep’, while Kalaignar stresses that on waking ‘he went nowhere, but leapt into my heart and settled there’. The couplet softens the reproach of 1217 into consolation. Pope: ‘And when I sleep he holds my form embraced; / And when I wake to fill my heart makes haste!’ Text identical on both sites.

tamil:
நனவினால் நல்காரை நோவர் கனவினால்
காதலர்க் காணா தவர்.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaarai noavar kanavinaal
kaadhalark kaanaa thavar.
current_meaning: Only women who never see their loved ones in dreams will complain about men who are not kind to them while they are awake.
elementary: Suppose your friend moved away, but you write letters every week. Someone who has never had a pen pal might say, ‘Your friend forgot you!’ But you know better, because you hear from them all the time. This woman says the same about her dreams: people who don’t have such dreams just don’t understand.
university: The heroine turns outward to defend her husband against criticism. Nōvar, ‘they grieve over / reproach’, has as subject kaṉaviṉāl kātalark kāṇātavar, ‘those who do not see their lovers through dreams’; nalkārai repeats the chapter’s epithet for the man who ‘shows no grace’. The implication is that her own dreams vindicate him, since he visits her every night. Commentators differ on whom she means: Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it general (‘women who do not see their lovers in dreams’), while Pappaiah specifies the young women of the town who are unmarried or have never known separation and so blame her husband as loveless. Pope: ‘In dreams who ne’er their lover’s form perceive, / For those in waking hours who show no love will grieve.’ Text identical on both sites.

tamil:
நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர் கனவினால்
காணார்கொல் இவ்வூ ரவர்.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal namneeththaar enpar kanavinaal
kaanaarkol ivvoo ravar.
current_meaning: The people of this town say he left me in waking life. Do they not see him coming to me in my dreams?
elementary: Imagine the neighbours saying, ‘Poor girl, her friend never visits.’ But every night her friend calls her on a secret walkie-talkie. She thinks, ‘They just can’t hear what I hear!’ That is how this woman feels about the town’s gossip.
university: The chapter closes by setting the heroine’s private knowledge against public opinion (alar, the town’s gossip that runs through the Kāmattuppāl). Nam nīttār eṉpar, ‘they say he has forsaken us’, reports the townsfolk’s verdict; ivvūravar, ‘the people of this town’, are the critics already glimpsed in 1219. The particle kol makes kāṇārkol a wondering question, ‘do they not see?’, which can be read two ways: Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take it as ‘do they not know that he visits me in dreams?’, whereas Kalaignar turns it back on the townsfolk, ‘do they never see their own departed lovers in dreams?’ Either way the dream, invisible to others, is her proof of his faithfulness. Pope: ‘They say, that he in waking hours has left me lone; / In dreams they surely see him not,- these people of the town.’ Text identical on both sites.

tamil:
மாலையோ அல்லை மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும்
வேலைநீ வாழி பொழுது.
transliteration:
Maalaiyo allai manandhaar uyirunnum
vaelainee vaazhi pozhudhu.
current_meaning: Long live you, evening! But you are not a gentle evening. You are a deadly time that eats up the lives of wives whose husbands are far away.
elementary: Think of the time of day you used to love most, like when a parent came home and played with you. If that parent had to go far away for a long time, the same hour might suddenly feel sad and heavy instead of happy. The wife in this verse feels that way about evening.
university: Chapter 123, poḻutu kaṇṭu iraṅkal (‘lamenting on seeing the hour’), belongs to the kaṟpiyal (wedded love) section: the wife, separated from her husband, finds that dusk (mālai), once the hour of reunion, now sharpens her grief. The opening couplet is an ironic apostrophe: vāḻi (‘may you live long!’) is a blessing turned to reproach, and maṇantār (‘those who were united/wedded’) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as women who knew union and now live apart. The key word vēlai is read two ways: Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it as ‘time, end-time’ (muṭivu kālam), while Mu. Karunanidhi reads vēl, ‘spear’, which is also Pope’s choice (‘a spear that doth devour / The souls of brides’). The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (the latter spells the chapter title as two words, poḻutukaṇṭu iraṅkal).

tamil:
புன்கண்ணை வாழி மருள்மாலை எம்கேள்போல்
வன்கண்ண தோநின் துணை.
transliteration:
Punkannai vaazhi marulmaalai emkaelpoal
vankanna dhoanin thunai.
current_meaning: Bless you, confused evening! Your eyes look dim and sad like mine. Is your partner as hard-hearted as my husband?
elementary: Sometimes when we are sad, the whole world seems sad with us: a grey sky looks like it is crying too. The wife looks at the fading evening light and asks it, kindly, ‘Did someone leave you too?’
university: Here the wife turns from accusing the evening to commiserating with it: mālai is marul (‘bewildered, dim’, the twilight in which day and night mingle, as Solomon Pappaiah explains) and puṉkaṇṇai (‘you have afflicted, dull eyes’), a picture of fading light as tear-dimmed sight. Kēḷ means a kinsman or intimate, here the husband, and vaṉkaṇṇatu (‘hard-eyed, pitiless’) mirrors puṉkaṇ: her eyes are sad because his are hard. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read the question as ‘is your companion too as merciless as my lover?’, while Pappaiah explicitly asks whether the evening’s husband is cruel like hers. Pope: ‘Thine eye is sad; Hail, doubtful hour of eventide! / Of cruel eye, as is my spouse, is too thy bride?’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பனிஅரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை துனிஅரும்பித்
துன்பம் வளர வரும்.
transliteration:
Paniarumpip paidhalkol maalai thuniarumpith
thunpam valara varum.
current_meaning: The pale evening comes, wet with drops of dew, and makes me feel tired of living. My sorrow keeps on growing.
elementary: Picture tiny dewdrops forming on leaves as the sun goes down. The wife says her sadness grows the same way, drop by drop, every evening, until it feels much bigger than it did in the morning.
university: The couplet is built on a parallel of two ‘buddings’: paṉi arumpi (dew forms like buds) and tuṉi arumpi (aversion or distress begins to sprout), so that the evening’s dew and the wife’s grief swell together. Paital koḷ describes the evening taking on a sallow, faded hue, recalling the wife’s own pasalai (love-pallor) of chapter 119. Commentators divide on time: Varadarasanar and Kesikan read the whole as the present evening, while Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi contrast an earlier evening that came ‘trembling and pale’ while the husband was near with the present one that brings mounting sorrow; Pope’s couplet explanation follows the latter (‘once came in with trembling and dimness’). Pope: ‘With buds of chilly dew wan evening’s shade enclose; / My anguish buds space and all my sorrow grows.’ Both web texts agree on the wording.

tamil:
காதலர் இல்வழி மாலை கொலைக்களத்து
ஏதிலர் போல வரும்.
transliteration:
Kaadhalar ilvazhi maalai kolaikkalaththu
aedhilar poala varum.
current_meaning: When my love is not here, evening comes at me like enemies marching onto a killing field.
elementary: Imagine a game where a scary character slowly walks toward you and you cannot run. When the wife is alone, the evening feels like that: it creeps closer and closer, and she dreads it.
university: The simile is military and stark: kolaikkaḷam is a ‘field of slaughter’ or execution ground, and ētilar are strangers or foes, so evening approaches the lonely wife like men coming to kill. Kesikan glosses ētilar as highway robbers (āṟalaippār) at a place of murder, Varadarasanar as enemies, and Karunanidhi shifts the image to an enemy’s raised sword; Solomon Pappaiah adds the contrast implicit in the chapter, that the same evening once made her life flourish when her husband was home. Pope’s couplet runs: ‘When absent is my love, the evening hour descends, / As when an alien host to field of battle wends.’ Both web sources give ētilar; a song setting by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net sings it as ētilār, a lyrical lengthening rather than a textual variant.

tamil:
காலைக்குச் செய்தநன்று என்கொல் எவன்கொல்யான்
மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை.
transliteration:
Kaalaikkuch cheydhanandru enkol evankolyaan
maalaikkuch cheydha pakai.
current_meaning: What good did I ever do for the morning, that it is gentle with me? And what wrong did I do to the evening, that it hurts me so much?
elementary: Have you ever felt that one part of the day is friendly and another part is mean to you? The wife feels mornings are kind and evenings are cruel, and she asks, puzzled, what she did to deserve it.
university: The couplet is a pair of rhetorical questions built on the parallel kālaikku / mālaikku (‘to the morning / to the evening’) and naṉṟu / pakai (‘a good turn / enmity’): the wife treats the two times of day as persons who repay her for imagined past conduct. Varadarasanar glosses pakai as ‘a hostile evil’ done to the evening, and Kalaignar adds the implied reason: love-pain grows sharpest when evening comes. The playful logic of reciprocity echoes the Kural’s ethical chapters on returning good for good, now applied absurdly to the hours. Pope: ‘O morn, how have I won thy grace? thou bring’st relief / O eve, why art thou foe! thou dost renew my grief.’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மாலைநோய் செய்தல் மணந்தார் அகலாத
காலை அறிந்த திலேன்.
transliteration:
Maalainoi seydhal manandhaar akalaadha
kaalai arindha thilaen.
current_meaning: While my husband had not yet left my side, I never knew how much pain evening could bring.
elementary: When your best friend is next to you, you do not notice how quiet the house is. Only when they go away do you notice the silence. The wife says she never knew evenings could hurt until her husband left.
university: The couplet turns on the contrast between maṇantār akalāta kālai (‘the time when he who wed me had not departed’) and the present, in which mālai nōy, ‘the evening sickness’, has made itself known. Kālai here is a pun: in the previous couplet it meant ‘morning’, but here it is the old Tamil word for ‘time, season’, a play the commentators make explicit by glossing it as kālam. Solomon Pappaiah stresses that the same evening once gave her joy; Varadarasanar and Kesikan read aṟintatilēṉ as ‘I did not know at all’. Pope: ‘The pangs that evening brings I never knew, / Till he, my wedded spouse, from me withdrew.’ Both web sources give the same text.

tamil:
காலை அரும்பிப் பகலெல்லாம் போதாகி
மாலை மலரும்இந் நோய்.
transliteration:
Kaalai arumpip pakalellaam poadhaaki
maalai malarumin noai.
current_meaning: This love-sickness starts as a tiny bud in the morning, grows bigger all day, and bursts into full flower in the evening.
elementary: Watch a flower: first a tiny bud, then a bigger bud, then it opens wide. The wife says her missing-him feeling grows the same way each day: small in the morning, bigger at noon, and wide open by evening.
university: One of the most admired images in the Kāmattuppāl, the couplet maps the growth of nōy (the love-sickness) onto the three stages of a flower: arumpu (bud) in the morning, pōtu (the full bud on the point of opening; Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it as pērarumpu, ‘large bud’) through the day, and malar (open bloom) at evening. The irony is pointed: the flower, symbol of love’s beauty, becomes the shape of love’s pain, and its daily cycle explains why the evening is worst. Solomon Pappaiah calls the disease ‘this flower of love-suffering’, and Karunanidhi generalises it to love itself. Pope: ‘My grief at morn a bud, all day an opening flower, / Full-blown expands in evening hour.’ The text is identical on both web sources.

tamil:
அழல்போலும் மாலைக்குத் தூதாகி ஆயன்
குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை.
transliteration:
Azhalpoalum maalaikkuth thoodhaaki aayan
kuzhalpoalum kollum padai.
current_meaning: Evening burns like fire, and the cowherd's flute is its messenger. Even that flute has become a weapon that kills me.
elementary: Sometimes a song you used to love can make you sad if it reminds you of someone who is far away. The herdsman plays his flute every evening; it used to sound sweet to the wife, but now it tells her that the lonely evening is coming, so it hurts to hear.
university: At dusk the herdsman (āyaṉ) plays his flute (kuḻal) as he brings the cattle home, and in classical Tamil poetics this belongs to the mullai landscape, whose mood is patient waiting (iruttal) and whose hour is evening. The flute becomes the tūtu (herald, envoy) of a mālai that burns like aḻal (fire), and so a paṭai (weapon) that kills; the repeated pōlum is read by the commentators as a particle of emphasis (‘the flute too’), not as ‘like’. Solomon Pappaiah notes that the flute once sounded sweet, and Karunanidhi likens its notes to the clang of a weapon. Pope: ‘The shepherd’s pipe is like a murderous weapon, to my ear, / For it proclaims the hour of ev’ning’s fiery anguish near.’ Both web sources give the same text.

tamil:
பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும் மதிமருண்டு
மாலை படர்தரும் போழ்து.
transliteration:
Padhimarundu paidhal uzhakkum madhimarundu
maalai padardharum poazhdhu.
current_meaning: When evening spreads over everything and confuses my mind, the whole town seems confused too, and suffers in sorrow just like me.
elementary: When you are very sad, it can feel as if the whole world is sad with you, even the street and the houses. As evening darkness spreads over the town, the wife feels that everyone there must be as unhappy as she is.
university: The couplet balances two phrases with maruṇṭu (‘bewildered, confused’): pati maruṇṭu, ‘the town bewildered’, and mati maruṇṭu, ‘the mind bewildered’, as evening ‘spreads’ (paṭartarum) over all. Varadarasanar, Kesikan and Karunanidhi take mati as ‘understanding’, so that the dusk confuses the mind and the whole town seems to share the wife’s grief; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that from now on the whole town will suffer as she has. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone takes mati as ‘moon’ (the moon itself bewildered), an alternative reading worth noting. Pope: ‘If evening’s shades, that darken all my soul, extend; / From this afflicted town will would of grief ascend.’ The text is identical on both web sources.

tamil:
பொருள்மாலை யாளரை உள்ளி மருள்மாலை
மாயும்என் மாயா உயிர்.
transliteration:
Porulmaalai yaalarai ulli marulmaalai
maayumen maayaa uyir.
current_meaning: I think of him, whose mind is set on earning money. In this confusing evening, my life, which has lasted until now, is dying away.
elementary: Imagine a parent who works far away to earn money for the family. Even if it is for a good reason, the child at home can feel very lonely at night. The wife feels this way: her husband went to earn wealth, and in the evening she misses him so much it feels unbearable.
university: The closing couplet names the cause of the separation: the husband is poruḷ-mālaiyāḷar, ‘one whose nature (mālai) is wealth’, who has gone away to earn; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens this to ‘one for whom the delusion of wealth is everything’. The poet plays on mālai three ways, ‘nature, disposition’ in poruḷmālai, ‘evening’ in maruḷ mālai (‘bewildering dusk’), and by sound with māyum (‘dies’) and māyā (‘undying’): the life that did not perish (māyā uyir) through the separation so far now perishes (māyum) at this dusk. Varadarasanar glosses māyā uyir as a life that ‘stood as if by magic’ despite grief. Pope: ‘This darkening eve, my darkling soul must perish utterly; / Remembering him who seeks for wealth, but seeks not me.’ Both web sources give identical text.

tamil:
சிறுமை நமக்கொழியச் சேட்சென்றார் உள்ளி
நறுமலர் நாணின கண்.
transliteration:
Sirumai namakkozhiyach chaetchendraar ulli
narumalar naanina kan.
current_meaning: Thinking of him who went far away and left you this sorrow, your eyes have cried away their beauty. Now they feel ashamed in front of the sweet-smelling flowers they once outshone.
elementary: Imagine a girl whose eyes were once as bright as the flowers in her garden. Her dearest person goes on a long trip, and she cries so much that her eyes become red and tired. Now when she looks at the fresh flowers, she feels shy, because the flowers look brighter than her eyes do.
university: Chapter 124, uṟuppu nalaṉ aḻital (‘the wasting of the beauty of the limbs’), continues the kaṟpiyal sequence on separation (pirivu): the wife, parted from her husband, loses her nalam (bodily loveliness) limb by limb, eyes, shoulders, bangles, forehead. Pope’s prose gloss (‘your eyes weep for him who is gone afar’) follows the traditional reading, associated with Parimelazhagar, in which the confidante (tōḻi) speaks to the heroine. The key words are ciṟumai (here ‘distress, grief’, glossed துன்பம் by Mu. Varadarasanar), cēṭ ceṉṟār (‘he who has gone far’), and naṟumalar nāṇiṉa kaṇ (‘the eyes were ashamed before fragrant flowers’): Sangam convention compares a woman’s eyes to blue water-lilies (kuvaḷai), so eyes that once shamed the flowers now hang back before them. Solomon Pappaiah reads ciṟumai as the ‘weakness of not bearing separation’ left with her while he bore it and went. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh writes the chapter title as one word (உறுப்புநலனழிதல்), thirukkural.net as two (உறுப்புநலன் அழிதல்).

tamil:
நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்
பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்.
transliteration:
Nayandhavar nalkaamai solluva poalum
pasandhu panivaarum kan.
current_meaning: My eyes have turned pale and keep filling with tears. They seem to tell everyone that the one I love is no longer kind to me.
elementary: When you are sad, you might try to hide it, but your red, teary eyes give you away, and people can guess something is wrong. The girl in this verse feels her pale, wet eyes are telling the whole town that the person she loves is far away and not caring for her right now.
university: The heroine imagines her eyes as informers: pasantu (‘having turned sallow’, from pacappu/pacalai, the greenish-yellow pallor of love-sickness that Chapter 119 treats at length) and paṉi vārum (‘streaming with dew’, i.e. tears) they ‘seem to speak’ (colluva pōlum) of nayantavar nalkāmai, the ‘unkindness’ or ‘failure to bestow grace’ of the one she desired. Nalkāmai is the negative of nalku, ‘to show favour, to be gracious’, a word used of kings and gods as well as lovers. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan add that the eyes tell this ‘to others’ (piṟarkku), which makes the poem about exposure as much as grief: the body betrays what modesty (nāṇ) would conceal. Pope renders: ‘The eye, with sorrow wan, all wet with dew of tears, / As witness of the lover’s lack of love appears.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்
மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்.
transliteration:
Thanandhamai saala arivippa poalum
manandha-naal veengiya thoal.
current_meaning: On our wedding day my shoulders were full and happy. Now they have grown thin, and they seem to tell everyone loudly that we are apart.
elementary: Think of a balloon at a birthday party, round and full, and then the same balloon a week later, small and wrinkled. The girl’s arms were full and strong when she was happy with the person she loves; now that he is away they have become thin, and anyone can see that she misses him.
university: The contrast is temporal and physical: maṇanta nāḷ (‘the day of union’, which may mean the wedding day or any day of togetherness) set against taṇantamai (‘the having-parted’, from taṇa, ‘to separate’). Vīṅkiya tōḷ (‘shoulders that swelled’) uses the Sangam convention that a woman’s tōḷ, shoulders or upper arms, grow plump (pūrittal) in happiness and thin in grief, so they become public evidence; cāla aṟivippa pōlum means ‘they seem to proclaim it fully’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all add that the thinning announces the separation ‘to others’, continuing the motif of 1232 in which the body exposes private grief. Pope: ‘These withered arms, desertion’s pangs abundantly display, / That swelled with joy on that glad nuptial day.’ Pope transliterates the compound as ‘manandha-naal’; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the Tamil text.

tamil:
பணைநீங்கிப் பைந்தொடி சோரும் துணைநீங்கித்
தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்.
transliteration:
Panai-neengip paindhoti soarum thunaineengith
tholkavin vaadiya thoal.
current_meaning: With your partner gone, your gold bangles slip off, and your shoulders have lost their old beauty and fullness.
elementary: Have you ever worn a ring or bracelet that fit perfectly, and then it got loose after you were sick for a while? In this verse, a girl is so sad that her loved one has gone away that she grows thin, and her bangles keep sliding off her arms.
university: The couplet builds a double loss with two parallel absolutives: paṇai nīṅki (‘the plumpness having gone’) and tuṇai nīṅki (‘the companion having gone’), so the departure of the tuṇai, the spouse, causes the departure of the paṇai, the fullness of the arm. Tolkaviṉ vāṭiya tōḷ means ‘shoulders whose former (tol) beauty (kaviṉ) has withered’, and pain̮toṭi cōrum, ‘the fresh-gold bangles slip down’, introduces the image of the loose bangle (toṭi, vaḷai) that dominates 1234-1236. The slipping bangle is a stock sign of separation in Sangam akam poetry and in Sanskrit kāvya alike. Pope’s gloss (‘In the absence of your consort, your shoulders… your bracelets… have become loose’) makes the confidante the speaker. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the shoulders as causing the bangles to slip; Kalaignar glosses paintoṭi as பசும்பொன் வளையல்கள். Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும் தொடியொடு
தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்.
transliteration:
Kotiyaar kodumai uraikkum thotiyodu
tholkavin vaadiya thoal.
current_meaning: My thin shoulders, their old beauty gone and their bangles slipping off, tell everyone how cruel the hard-hearted one was to me.
elementary: Sometimes our bodies tell a story we don’t say out loud, like a droopy face when we’re upset. Here the girl’s thin arms and falling bangles seem to tell the whole town, “Look how much he has hurt her by staying away so long.”
university: Koṭiyār koṭumai uraikkum (‘they speak the cruelty of the cruel one’) is an emphatic figura etymologica: koṭiyār (‘the cruel/crooked one’, honorific plural used of the husband) and koṭumai (‘cruelty’) share the root koṭu, ‘bent, harsh’. The second line repeats 1234’s tolkaviṉ vāṭiya tōḷ verbatim, a deliberate echo, while toṭiyoṭu (‘together with the bangles’) makes the slipping bracelets co-witnesses. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses koṭiyār as ‘the cruel one who does not feel my suffering’; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the shoulders say it ‘for the town to know’ (ūraṟiya). The accusation is ventured here only to be withdrawn in 1236, where the heroine is pained to hear him so called. Pope: ‘These wasted arms, the bracelet with their wonted beauty gone, / The cruelty declare of that most cruel one.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தொடியொடு தோள்நெகிழ நோவல் அவரைக்
கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து.
transliteration:
Thotiyodu thoalnekizha noval avaraik
kotiyar enakkooral nondhu.
current_meaning: Because my bangles slip and my shoulders are thin, people call him cruel. Hearing him blamed hurts me more than my own pain.
elementary: Imagine your best friend moves away for a while, and you are sad. If someone says, “Your friend is mean for leaving you,” you might feel even worse, because you still love your friend and don’t want anyone to speak badly of them. That is how the girl in this verse feels.
university: Here the tone turns: after 1235’s accusation, the heroine is pained (nōval, ‘I grieve’) when others, or the confidante, call him koṭiyar (‘cruel’) because of her loosened bangles and thinned shoulders (toṭiyoṭu tōḷ nekiḻa). The final word nontu (‘in sorrow, being hurt’) can be taken with the speakers or with the heroine, and the commentators divide: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar have the onlookers (kāṇpavar) say it, while Solomon Pappaiah makes the shoulders and bangles themselves the speakers. Pope’s gloss (‘I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man’) addresses the confidante, which accords with the reading associated with Parimelazhagar that the heroine answers her tōḻi. The ethic is the wife’s loyalty (kaṟpu), which forbids hearing the husband reproached even when she is the one who suffers. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே கொடியார்க்கென்
வாடுதோட் பூசல் உரைத்து.
transliteration:
Paadu perudhiyo nenje kotiyaarkken
vaatudhot poosal uraiththu.
current_meaning: My heart, why not go to that hard-hearted man and tell him how loudly my thin shoulders cry out? Wouldn't that bring you praise?
elementary: Sometimes when we miss someone, we talk to ourselves, like “Come on, brave heart, go tell them how we feel!” The girl in this verse talks to her own heart and asks it to go to the person she loves and tell him how sad and thin she has become.
university: The heroine now addresses her own nenjam (heart, mind) as a possible messenger, a device developed at length in the next chapter, 125 (neñcoṭu kiḷattal, ‘speaking to the heart’). Pāṭu peṟutiyō means ‘will you gain greatness/glory?’; the question can be read as an exhortation (Kalaignar: ‘will you not gain glory?’) or as a rueful challenge (Solomon Pappaiah: ‘will you gain glory by telling him these empty rumours?’). Vāṭu tōḷ pūcal is ‘the clamour of my withering shoulders’, pūcal being a noisy outcry or public uproar, so the wasting body is imagined as shouting. Koṭiyārkku (‘to the cruel one’) resumes the word the heroine resisted in 1236, which Mu. Varadarasanar softens to ‘the one who is called cruel’. Pope: ‘My heart! say ought of glory wilt thou gain, / If to that cruel one thou of thy wasted arms complain?’ Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text, including the sandhi form வாடுதோட் பூசல்.

tamil:
முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது
பைந்தொடிப் பேதை நுதல்.
transliteration:
Muyangiya kaikalai ookkap pasandhadhu
paindhotip paedhai nudhal.
current_meaning: Once, when I only loosened my arms from our hug, the forehead of my innocent wife with her gold bangles turned pale at once.
elementary: Imagine a little child holding a parent’s hand at a busy fair. If the parent lets go for just a second, the child’s face might look worried right away. The husband in this verse remembers that his wife looked worried and pale even when he let go of a hug for just a moment, so he knows how much she must be missing him now that he is far away.
university: With 1238 the voice changes: Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar gloss in the husband’s first person (‘when I loosened my arms’), and the traditional reading has the talaivaṉ, away from home, recalling his wife’s fragility to explain why he must hurry back. Muyaṅkiya kaikaḷai ūkka is ‘when [I] loosened (ūkka, ‘to slacken, withdraw’) the arms that embraced’; pacantatu… nutal, ‘the forehead turned sallow’, applies pacappu, the pallor of love-longing, to her brow, the classic site of a woman’s brightness (oḷ nutal, 1240). Paintoṭip pētai, ‘the innocent one with fresh-gold bangles’, uses pētai, ‘young, guileless woman’, a tender term. The logic is a fortiori: if a moment’s slackening paled her, what must long absence do? Solomon Pappaiah adds that he loosened his grip fearing his tight hold would hurt her. Pope: ‘One day the fervent pressure of embracing arms I checked, / Grew wan the forehead of the maid with golden armlet decked.’ Text identical on both sites.

tamil:
முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழப் பசப்புற்ற
பேதை பெருமழைக் கண்.
transliteration:
Muyakkidaith thanvali poazhap pasapputra
paedhai perumazhaik kan.
current_meaning: When even a little breeze slipped in between us as we hugged, the big, cool eyes of my innocent wife turned pale.
elementary: Think of two friends sitting so close on a cold night that not even the wind can get between them. If a tiny gust slips in, one of them shivers. The husband here remembers that even a little breeze between them made his wife look sad, so he knows a long trip away must be very hard for her.
university: The husband’s recollection continues and intensifies 1238: now not his arms but a cool breeze (taṇ vaḷi) ‘split’ (pōḻa, ‘to cleave, pierce’) their embrace (muyakku iṭai, ‘in the midst of the embrace’), and at that hair’s-breadth separation her eyes, not her forehead, were touched with pacappu. Perumaḻaik kaṇ, ‘large rain-eyes’, is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘large eyes like rain’ (cool and moist) and by Kalaignar as ‘wide, long eyes’; the image may suggest both their coolness and their readiness for tears. Solomon Pappaiah ends his gloss with the husband’s worried question, ‘how must they be now?’, which captures the a fortiori logic of 1238-1240. Pope: ‘As we embraced a breath of wind found entrance there; / The maid’s large liquid eyes were dimmed with care.’ Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text.

tamil:
கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே
ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு.
transliteration:
Kannin pasappoa paruvaral eydhindrae
onnudhal seydhadhu kandu.
current_meaning: Her bright forehead turned pale first. Did the paleness in her eyes see this and become even sadder?
elementary: When one person in a family is sad, the others often feel sad too, just from seeing them. In this verse the husband imagines his wife’s face as a little family: when her forehead turned pale, her eyes saw it and became even sadder.
university: The closing couplet is a conceit (taṟkuṟippēṟṟa aṇi, poetic fancy) in which parts of the wife’s face react to one another. Kaṇṇiṉ pacappō paruvaral eytiṉṟē, ‘did the pallor of the eyes fall into distress?’, uses the particle ō for wondering doubt, and oṇ nutal ceytatu kaṇṭu, ‘having seen what the bright forehead did’, refers back to 1238, where the forehead paled first. Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar read: seeing the forehead turn sallow, the pallor of her eyes grew into greater suffering. Solomon Pappaiah offers a different reading, in which the eye, once ashamed before the forehead’s delicacy, now shares its distress. The chapter thus ends where it began, with the eyes (1231), now joined by the forehead, so that the ‘wasting of the limbs’ is complete from head to arm. Pope: ‘The dimness of her eye felt sorrow now, / Beholding what was done by that bright brow.’ Text identical on both sites; ytamizh’s transliteration renders the archaic eytiṉṟē as ‘eydhindrae’.

tamil:
நினைத்தொன்று சொல்லாயோ நெஞ்சே எனைத்தொன்றும்
எவ்வநோய் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து.
transliteration:
Ninaiththondru sollaayo nenje enaiththondrum
evvanoai theerkkum marundhu.
current_meaning: My heart, won't you think hard and tell me some medicine, any medicine at all, that can cure this sickness of sorrow that nothing else can cure?
elementary: Imagine you miss someone so much that it feels like a tummy ache that no medicine can fix. So you talk to yourself: “Come on, heart, you are clever, think of something that will make me feel better!”
university: Chapter 125, neñcoṭu kiḷattal (‘speaking with one’s heart’), belongs to the kaṟpiyal (wedded-love) section: the wife, alone in separation (pirivu), turns her own neñcu (heart/mind) into a confidant and argues with it, a device Pope renders ‘Soliloquy’. The key compound evvanōy joins evvam (‘distress, sorrow’) with nōy (‘disease’), and enaittonṟum (‘whatever it may be, of any kind’) stresses that she will accept any remedy at all; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the sickness as grown out of love (காதலால் வளர்ந்த), and Kalaignar as kātal nōy ‘incurable by any medicine’. The commentary tradition reads the opening ninaittu onṟu collāyō as a plea to the heart, the one faculty still ‘with’ her, to think on her behalf. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the chapter title is printed as one word (நெஞ்சொடுகிளத்தல்) on ytamizh and as நெஞ்சோடு கிளத்தல் (long ō) on thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காதல் அவரிலர் ஆகநீ நோவது
பேதைமை வாழியென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Kaadhal avarilar aakanee noavadhu
paedhaimai vaazhiyen nenju.
current_meaning: Long live you, my heart! He has no love for us, so your suffering over him is just foolish.
elementary: Imagine you keep waiting by the door for a friend who has forgotten all about you. You might say to yourself, “Silly heart, why are you sad about someone who isn’t even thinking about you?”
university: The heroine now scolds her heart: kātal avar ilar āka (‘he being without love’), nī nōvatu (‘your aching’) is pētaimai (‘folly, simple-mindedness’, from pētai ‘simpleton’). The interjection vāḻi eṉ neñcu (‘long may you live, my heart!’) is a conventional blessing that here carries gentle irony, as Solomon Pappaiah’s rendering ‘நீ வாழ்ந்து போ’ makes explicit. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss pētaimai as aṟiyāmai (ignorance), and Pope translates ‘thy smart is folly, fare thee well my heart’. The traditional reading, which modern commentators follow, takes the accusation of lovelessness as the wife’s overstatement in grief rather than a settled judgment of her husband. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இருந்துள்ளி என்பரிதல் நெஞ்சே பரிந்துள்ளல்
பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Irundhulli enparidhal nenje parindhullal
paidhalnoai seydhaarkan il.
current_meaning: My heart, why stay here thinking of him and suffering? The one who gave us this sickness of sorrow has no kind thoughts for us.
elementary: Think of sitting by the window all day thinking about a friend who moved away, while that friend is busy and not thinking about you. You might ask yourself, “Why am I sitting here feeling sad when they aren’t even missing me?”
university: The heart is questioned for sitting idle: iruntu uḷḷi (‘remaining here and thinking’) eṉ paritaltal (‘why grieve?’), while parintu uḷḷal (‘thinking with tender pity’) is absent in the one who caused paital nōy (‘the sickness of sorrow’; paital = distress). Solomon Pappaiah unpacks iruntu as ‘neither going to where he is, nor dying here’, a reading that sharpens the reproach of passive pining. Pope’s explanation on ytamizh.com prints ‘there are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him’, which looks like a transcription slip for ‘loving thoughts’; all four Tamil glosses render parintu uḷḷal as anpu or irakkam (love, pity). The commentary tradition treats the line as the heroine voicing a suspicion she does not finally believe. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி நெஞ்சே இவையென்னைத்
தின்னும் அவர்க்காணல் உற்று.
transliteration:
Kannum kolachchaeri nenje ivaiyennaith
thinnum avarkkaanal utru.
current_meaning: My heart, when you go to him, take my eyes with you too. They want so badly to see him that they are eating me alive.
elementary: Imagine your heart can fly to visit someone you miss, but your eyes are stuck at home and keep crying because they want to see that person too. So you say, “Heart, please take my eyes with you, they won’t stop bothering me!”
university: This couplet presupposes that the heart has already gone to the absent husband (a convention developed in neighbouring couplets), so the heroine asks it to take the eyes too: kaṇṇum koḷa (‘taking the eyes also’) cēṟi (‘you will go’). The eyes, left behind, ivai eṉṉait tiṉṉum (‘these devour me’) avar kāṇal uṟṟu (‘set on seeing him’); Mu. Varadarasanar glosses tiṉṉum as பிடுங்கித் தின்கின்றன (‘pluck and eat’), and Pappaiah softens it to ‘grieve as though eating me’. The image of a body divided against itself, heart travelling while eyes torment the one who stays, extends the Kāmattuppāl motif of personified eyes (compare chapter 118, kaṇ vitumpu aḻital). Pope renders the line ‘O rid me of these eyes, my heart’. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
செற்றார் எனக்கை விடல்உண்டோ நெஞ்சேயாம்
உற்றால் உறாஅ தவர்.
transliteration:
Setraar enakkai vidtalundo nenjaeyaam
utraal uraaa thavar.
current_meaning: My heart, he does not come to us even when we long for him. But can we really give him up, saying, "He hates us"?
elementary: Imagine a friend who hasn’t called you back in a long time. You could decide, “They don’t like me anymore, I’ll forget them,” but deep down you know you can’t stop caring about them.
university: The heroine tests the idea of abandoning her husband and rejects it: ceṟṟār eṉa (‘saying he is one who hates us’, from ceṟu ‘to hate, be hostile’) kaiviṭal uṇṭō (‘is there such a thing as letting go?’). The second line contrasts yām uṟṟāl (‘though we draw close, long for him’) with uṟāatavar (‘he who does not draw close’), the lengthened uṟāa being an alapeṭai (prosodic lengthening) for metre. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the question as rhetorical (‘can we give him up?’), whereas Pappaiah turns it toward her own will (‘do I have the firmness of heart to give him up?’). The couplet thus marks the chapter’s turn from reproaching the heart to confessing its constancy. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கலந்துணர்த்தும் காதலர்க் கண்டாற் புலந்துணராய்
பொய்க்காய்வு காய்திஎன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Kalandhunarththum kaadhalark kandaar pulandhunaraai
poikkaaivu kaaidhi-en nenju.
current_meaning: My heart, when you see the one you love, who ends our quarrels with a hug, you cannot even stay upset. So the anger you show him now is fake.
elementary: Imagine pretending to be cross with your best friend, but the moment they come and give you a hug, you start smiling. So you tell yourself, “I’m not really angry, I’m just pretending!”
university: The couplet turns on the Tamil love-poetry concept of ūṭal / pulavi (a lover’s feigned sulking that is meant to be dissolved): the husband is one who kalantu uṇarttum (‘removes the sulk by union’), and when the heart sees him it does not pulantu uṇar (‘sulk and then make up’) at all. Hence its present anger is poykkāyvu (‘false heat, sham anger’, from kāy ‘to burn, be angry’) that it kāyti (‘burns with’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow this reading closely, while Solomon Pappaiah expands it into an exhortation: ‘give up this pretended hatred and go to him’. The couplet anticipates the later chapters on pulavi (131-133). Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (both read kaṇṭāṟ with the sandhi ṟ).

tamil:
காமம் விடுஒன்றோ நாண்விடு நன்னெஞ்சே
யானோ பொறேன்இவ் விரண்டு.
transliteration:
Kaamam viduondroa naanvidu nannenjae
yaanoa poraen-iv virandu.
current_meaning: My good heart, either let go of your love or let go of your shyness. I cannot carry both of them at once.
elementary: Imagine wanting very badly to tell someone how much you miss them, but feeling too shy to say it. Holding both feelings at once is hard, so you tell yourself, “Either stop missing them, or stop being shy and just tell them!”
university: This is the chapter’s best-known dilemma: kāmam viṭu oṉṟō (‘either let go of desire’) nāṇ viṭu (‘or let go of modesty’), for yāṉō poṟēṉ iv iraṇṭu (‘I cannot bear these two together’). Nāṇ (modesty, shame) is a defining virtue of the Tamil heroine, which normally forbids her from going to the man or declaring her longing; kāmam here means love-desire, not merely physical lust. The heart is called naṉṉeñcu (‘good heart’), a coaxing address. Kalaignar makes the conflict explicit (desire drives her to speak, modesty stops her), and Pappaiah stresses that the two pull in opposite directions; Pope renders it ‘Or bid thy love, or bid thy shame depart’. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பரிந்தவர் நல்காரென்று ஏங்கிப் பிரிந்தவர்
பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Parindhavar nalkaarendru aengip pirindhavar
pinselvaai paedhaien nenju.
current_meaning: My foolish heart, you are sad that he will not feel sorry for us and be kind. Yet you still run after the one who left us.
elementary: Imagine saying, “My friend doesn’t care about me!” and then running after that same friend anyway. You might laugh at yourself: “Silly heart, you complain about them and then follow them everywhere!”
university: The heart is again called pētai (‘simpleton’), now for a contradiction: it laments (ēṅki) that the husband, out of pity (parintu), nalkār (‘will not show favour’), yet it goes piṉ cel (‘following behind’) the one who has pirintavar (‘parted’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the line as exposing the heart’s inconsistency; Solomon Pappaiah gives the more sympathetic reading that the heart follows him to tell him of her suffering, which he simply does not know. The verb nalku (‘to bestow grace, be kind’) is a key word of Tamil love poetry, often used of the hero’s favour to the heroine. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தார் காத லவரால் உள்ளிநீ
யாருழைச் சேறியென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ullaththaar kaadha lavaraal ulli-nee
yaaruzhaich cheriyaen nenju.
current_meaning: My heart, the one we love lives right here inside you. So when you think of him, where are you going to look for him?
elementary: Imagine searching the whole house for your favourite toy while holding it in your hand the whole time. The Kural says the same to the heart: “The person you miss is already inside you, why go looking for them outside?”
university: The heroine catches her heart in a paradox: kātalavar uḷḷattār āl (‘the beloved is in the heart’, with āl as an emphatic particle), so when nī uḷḷi (‘you, thinking of him’) set off, yār uḻai cēṟi (‘to whom will you go?’; uḻai = ‘to the side of, to the place of’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as ‘to whom do you go searching, when he is within?’; Pope gives ‘Roaming, whom dost thou think to find?’. The line is a rare moment of consolation in the chapter, and has often been read devotionally, the beloved dwelling in the heart being a common image in Tamil bhakti. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints a spaced kāta lavarāl).

tamil:
துன்னாத் துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா
இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்.
transliteration:
Thunnaath thurandhaarai nenjaththu udaiyaemaa
innum izhaththum kavin.
current_meaning: If we keep in our heart the one who left us and does not come near, we will lose even more of the beauty we have left.
elementary: Imagine thinking all day about a friend who went away and never visits. The more you think about it, the more tired and sad you look. So you tell yourself, “If I keep holding on like this, I’ll lose even more of my sparkle.”
university: The closing couplet weighs the cost of constancy: tuṉṉāt tuṟantārai (‘him who, not drawing near, has left us’; tuṉṉu ‘to approach, be joined’, tuṟa ‘to leave, renounce’) neñcattu uṭaiyēmā (‘if we hold in the heart’), iṉṉum iḻattum kaviṉ (‘we shall lose still more of our beauty’). Kaviṉ is beauty or comeliness, linking back to chapter 124 on the wasting of the limbs. Solomon Pappaiah draws out the force of iṉṉum (‘still more’): having already lost her outer beauty, she will now lose her inner beauty too, a reading echoed in Pope’s ‘further loss of dignity’. The line ends the soliloquy on the heroine’s awareness that her loyalty is consuming her, without any resolve to give it up. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும்
நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு.
transliteration:
Kaamak kanichchi utaikkum niraiyennum
naanuththaazh veezhththa kadhavu.
current_meaning: My self-control was like a door locked tight with the bolt of shyness. But the axe of love smashes that door down.
elementary: Imagine a girl who keeps her feelings locked behind a strong door, with shyness as the bolt. But her love for someone is like a big axe, and one swing breaks the whole door open. Feelings that strong cannot stay locked away.
university: Chapter 126, niṟai aḻital (‘the breaking of reserve’), opens with the heroine (talaivi), parted from her husband, admitting that the self-command she prized has given way. The image is architectural: niṟai (reserve, the firmness that keeps inner feeling from showing) is the door (katavu), nāṇ (modesty, shame) is the bolt (tāḻ) that holds it, and kāmam (love-longing) is the kaṇicci, a heavy axe or pick, which breaks it; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss kaṇicci as an axe (கோடாலி/கோடரி). In the reading associated with Parimelazhagar, niṟai is the faculty that guards what should be kept within and nāṇ is its fastening, so the couplet states the chapter’s claim that love overpowers both together. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. Textual note: ytamizh.com’s English ‘Couplet Explanation’ for 1251 (‘My precious life is saved by the raise of rumour…’) does not fit this couplet and appears to be misplaced from another kural; its Pope couplet (‘The axe of lust can break the door of chastity…’) is the relevant rendering.

tamil:
காமம் எனவொன்றோ கண்ணின்றென் நெஞ்சத்தை
யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Kaamam enavondroa kannindren nenjaththai
yaamaththum aalum thozhil.
current_meaning: This thing called love has no pity. Even at midnight, it keeps giving orders to my heart.
elementary: Think of a strict boss who makes you work even in the middle of the night while everyone else is asleep. The heroine says love is like that boss: it never lets her heart rest, not even at midnight.
university: The heroine personifies kāmam as a harsh ruler: kaṇ iṉṟu means ‘without kaṇṇōṭṭam’ (without kindly regard, pitiless), as Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதது), and yāmattum āḷum toḻil is ‘the work of ruling even at yāmam’, the dead of night. Solomon Pappaiah draws out the image of a master who makes a servant toil at midnight while all others sleep, which sharpens the chapter’s theme: niṟai cannot survive a power that never rests. The phrase eṉa oṉṟō (‘this one thing called…’) carries a note of exasperated contempt in the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads kaṇ iṉṟu as ‘standing in the eye’ (கண்ணில் நின்று), a minority interpretation. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மறைப்பேன்மன் காமத்தை யானோ குறிப்பின்றித்
தும்மல்போல் தோன்றி விடும்.
transliteration:
Maraippaenman kaamaththai yaanoa kurippindrith
thummalpoal thoandri vidum.
current_meaning: I try to hide my love, but it gives no warning. Like a sneeze, it just bursts out.
elementary: Have you ever tried to stop a sneeze in a quiet room? You hold your nose, but out it comes anyway. The heroine says her love is like that: she tries to keep it secret, but it pops out all by itself.
university: The homely simile of the sneeze (tummal) is one of the most memorable images in the Kāmattuppāl: the heroine would conceal (maṟaippēṉ) her kāmam, but it appears kuṟippiṉṟi, ‘without regard to my intention’ or ‘without warning’. The particle maṉ in maṟaippēṉmaṉ marks an intention that fails (‘I would indeed hide it, but…’), a construction repeated in 1254 (eṉpēṉmaṉ). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses kuṟippiṉṟi as ‘not staying as I intend’ (என் குறிப்பின்படி நிற்காமல்), while Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘without my even knowing’, stressing involuntariness. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘like a sneeze / It shows itself, and gives no warning sign’) keeps the image. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன் யானோஎன் காமம்
மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyutaiyaen enpaenman yaanoa-en kaamam
maraiyirandhu mandru patum.
current_meaning: I used to say I had strong self-control. But my love has come out of hiding and now shows itself for everyone to see.
elementary: Imagine being sure you could keep a big secret, and then finding the whole town talking about it. The heroine thought she was strong enough to keep her love quiet, but now everyone can see it.
university: The heroine contrasts what she used to say (niṟaiyuṭaiyēṉ eṉpēṉmaṉ, ‘I would say I have reserve’, the maṉ again marking a claim now undone) with what happens: her kāmam, passing beyond concealment (maṟai iṟantu), appears in the maṉṟu, the village common or assembly place. The word maṉṟu makes the exposure social: her longing is now matter for public talk, recalling the alar (gossip) of chapter 115. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss maṉṟam as the public assembly; Solomon Pappaiah renders the result as ‘known to the townspeople’ (ஊரவர் அறிய). Pope’s English on ytamizh.com (‘In womanly reserve I deemed myself beyond assail; / But love will come abroad, and casts away the veil’) brings out the gendered sense of niṟai in the commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar. The couplet is identical on both sources.

tamil:
செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை காமநோய்
உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Setraarpin sellaap perundhakaimai kaamanoai
utraar aRivadhondru andru.
current_meaning: People sick with love do not know the self-respect that refuses to run after someone who has turned away from them.
elementary: When a friend walks away from you, pride might say, ‘Fine, I won’t chase after them.’ But the heroine says that when you love someone very much, that kind of pride disappears, and you want to follow them anyway.
university: Ceṟṟār, literally ‘those who hate’ or ‘enemies’, is here the husband who has gone away, seen through the heroine’s hurt as one who has spurned her; peruntakaimai is the noble self-respect (Mu. Varadarasanar: மானத்தோடு நிற்கும் பெருந்தகைமை) of not following such a person. Kāmanōy uṟṟār, ‘those who have caught the sickness of love’, do not know that dignity, so the couplet extends the chapter’s theme from concealment to pride. Commentators divide on the logic: Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take it as a direct statement that the lovesick lack such dignity, Solomon Pappaiah turns it around (only those who have not known love can manage it), and Kalaignar stresses that the lovesick cannot treat the departed lover as an enemy. In the reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the heroine is explaining to her confidante why she cannot simply hold her ground. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
செற்றவர் பின்சேறல் வேண்டி அளித்தரோ
எற்றென்னை உற்ற துயர்.
transliteration:
Setravar pinsaeral vaendi aliththaroa
etrennai utra thuyar.
current_meaning: How strange is this sorrow that has taken hold of me! It makes me want to follow the very one who turned away from me.
elementary: Sometimes when a friend goes away, we feel so sad that we want to run after them, even if they did not say a kind goodbye. The heroine wonders at this sadness: it is so strong that it makes her want to follow him anyway.
university: The heroine marvels at her own grief: eṟṟu (‘of what kind?’) and the exclamatory aḷittarō, which can be heard ironically as ‘how gracious!’, frame a sorrow (tuyar) that makes her wish to go after (piṉ cēṟal) ceṟṟavar, the one who has scorned or left her. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘My grief how full of grace, I pray you see! / It seeks to follow him that hateth me’) captures this irony. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan treat tuyar as the kāmanōy (love-sickness) itself, and Solomon Pappaiah calls it exceedingly cruel because it drives her to follow. The couplet continues 1255: having denied that she has the dignity not to follow, the heroine now wonders at the grief that compels her. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
நாணென ஒன்றோ அறியலம் காமத்தால்
பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்.
transliteration:
Naanena ondroa ariyalam kaamaththaal
paeniyaar petpa seyin.
current_meaning: When the one I love, out of love, does the things I long for, I no longer know anything called shyness.
elementary: When someone you love is kind to you and does just what you hoped, you forget to be shy around them. You just feel happy and close. The heroine says that is how she feels when her husband shows his love.
university: Here nāṇ (shyness, modesty) is not broken by force but forgotten: when pēṇiyār (the one I cherish) does peṭpa (what I desire) out of kāmam, ‘we do not know anything called shame’ (nāṇ eṉa oṉṟō aṟiyalam). The plural aṟiyalam can be inclusive (‘we women’) or the heroine’s own, and commentators differ on tense: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it conditionally (‘if he does…, we shall not know’), Solomon Pappaiah as past experience (‘when he did… I did not know shame’). Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘No sense of shame my gladdened mind shall prove, / When he returns my longing heart to bless with love’) takes it as a hope for his return. Read within the chapter, the couplet explains why reserve fails: in the presence of a loving husband, nāṇ has no place. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
