பன்மாயக் கள்வன் பணிமொழி அன்றோநம்
பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை.
transliteration:
Panmaayak kalvan panimozhi androa-nam
penmai udaikkum padai.
current_meaning: My love is a clever thief with many tricks. Aren't his soft, sweet words the army that breaks down my firmness as a woman?
elementary: Imagine building a strong sandcastle wall, and then a friend says something so sweet and kind that you happily knock the wall down yourself. The heroine says her husband’s gentle words are like that: they break down her strong ‘I won’t give in’ feeling.
university: The heroine calls her beloved pal-māyak kaḷvaṉ, ‘a thief of many wiles’, an affectionate reproach familiar from Tamil love poetry, and names his paṇimoḻi (humble, coaxing words) as the paṭai (army, weapon) that breaks her peṇmai (womanliness, here the firmness that resists). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peṇmai as a fortress (அரண்) and Solomon Pappaiah as the fort of self-restraint (மன அடக்கமாகிய கோட்டை), sustaining the military image of breaking. Puliyur Kesikan reads the couplet as past (‘were they not, on that day…’), referring to their courtship, while others read it as a present truth. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘The words of that deceiver, versed in every wily art, / Are instruments that break through every guard of woman’s heart!’) pushes kaḷvaṉ toward ‘deceiver’, though the Tamil glosses keep the tone fond and playful. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
புலப்பல் எனச்சென்றேன் புல்லினேன் நெஞ்சம்
கலத்தல் உறுவது கண்டு.
transliteration:
Pulappal enachchendraen pullinaen nenjam
kalaththal uruvadhu kandu.
current_meaning: I went to him meaning to sulk and hold back. But when I saw my heart already rushing to join him, I hugged him.
elementary: Imagine planning to stay grumpy with a friend who came back late. But when you see them, your heart feels so happy that you forget to be grumpy and give them a big hug instead. That is what happened to the heroine.
university: The couplet turns on the Tamil love convention of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking or feigned pique): pulappal, ‘I will sulk’, was her plan, but pulliṉēṉ, ‘I embraced’, was the result, because she saw her neñcam (heart) already beginning kalattal (union, mingling) with him. The heart acting independently of the self continues the preceding chapter, neñcoṭu kiḷattal (‘speaking to one’s heart’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘my heart leaving me and joining him’, and Solomon Pappaiah elaborates that she stepped away to sulk but, seeing her heart go to him without restraint, gave up and embraced him. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss gives an allegorical (yogic) reading, a minority view. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; Pope’s rendering there (‘I’ll shun his greeting’; saying thus with pride away I went: / I held him in my arms, for straight I felt my heart relent) follows the standard reading.

tamil:
நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்க்கு உண்டோ
புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
Ninandheeyil ittanna nenjinaarkku undoa
punarndhoodi niRpaem enal.
current_meaning: Can those whose hearts melt like fat thrown into a fire ever say, "We will be close to him and still keep up our sulking"?
elementary: Put a pat of butter in a hot pan and it melts almost at once. The heroine says her heart is like that butter: the moment her husband is near, she cannot stay cross with him.
university: The chapter closes with a vivid simile: niṇam tīyil iṭṭaṉṉa neñciṉār, ‘those whose hearts are like fat (niṇam) put into fire’, cannot say puṇarntu ūṭi niṟpēm, ‘we will unite and yet stand firm in ūṭal (sulking)’. Commentators differ over the construction: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘can those like me, with melting hearts, keep up a sulk once they have agreed to it’, Kalaignar takes it as ‘can they hold firm in sulking after having been together’, and Solomon Pappaiah expands it into a general statement about women whose hearts melt at the sight of their lovers. The couplet answers 1259 in general form and closes the chapter’s argument: with a heart like this, no niṟai can last. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the musical setting by P.A. Muthukrishnan reproduced on thirukkural.net paraphrases the image as butter in the flame (தழலிடை வெண்ணெய்).

tamil:
வாளற்றுப் புற்கென்ற கண்ணும் அவர்சென்ற
நாளொற்றித் தேய்ந்த விரல்.
transliteration:
Vaalatrup purkendra kannum avarsendra
naalotrith thaeyndha viral.
current_meaning: My eyes have lost their shine from watching the road for him. My fingers are worn out from touching the marks I made to count the days since he left.
elementary: Imagine someone you love goes on a long trip. Every day you stand at the window looking down the road, and every night you make a mark on the wall and count them all again. After many days your eyes are tired from looking and your finger is sore from counting. That is how much the lady in this verse misses her husband.
university: Chapter 127, avarvayiṉ vitumpal (‘eager longing for him’; vitumpal = impatient yearning), continues the kaṟpu (wedded love) section: the time the husband (talaivaṉ) fixed for his return is passing, and the wife (talaivi) speaks her impatience; in two couplets (1268, 1270) the husband’s own eagerness is voiced, which is why Pope titles the chapter ‘Mutual Desire’. Here the heroine offers two physical proofs: her eyes are vāḷ aṟṟu (stripped of their lustre, vāḷ = brightness) and puṟkeṉṟa (dimmed, unable to see fine things, as Solomon Pappaiah glosses), and her finger is worn from nāḷ oṟṟi, pressing the day-marks she has drawn on the wall; Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply the wall (சுவர்) on which the days are scored. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the heroine telling her friend (tōḻi) that she can no longer bear the delay. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இலங்கிழாய் இன்று மறப்பின்என் தோள்மேல்
கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து.
transliteration:
Ilangizhaai indru marappin-en thoalmael
kalangazhiyum kaarikai neeththu.
current_meaning: My friend in shining jewels, if I forgot him even now, my arms would lose their beauty and my bangles would slip off.
elementary: A girl tells her best friend: “Even though missing him hurts, I won’t stop thinking about him. If I tried to forget him, I would only become sadder and thinner, so thin that my bracelets would fall off.” Remembering him, even when it is hard, is what keeps her going.
university: The heroine addresses her friend as ilaṅkiḻāy, ‘you of shining ornaments’ (Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the addressee as the tōḻi; Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss ஒளிரும் நகை அணிந்தவனே uses a masculine ending, apparently a slip). Kalam aḻiyum (‘the ornaments come off’) is the stock Tamil sign of a wasting body: the arms (tōḷ) grow thin and the bangles slide off, and kārikai (beauty, grace) departs. The logic is a reversal: one might expect forgetting to ease her pain, but she says that even to try to forget him today would ruin her further, so she chooses to keep remembering. The Drew/Lazarus explanation printed on ytamizh.com reads ‘even in the other life’, reflecting a reading of iṉṟu that some commentators extend; the main modern glosses take iṉṟu simply as ‘today, while I suffer’. The Tamil text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்
வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்.
transliteration:
Urannasaii ullam thunaiyaakach chendraar
varalnasaii innum ulen.
current_meaning: He went away to win success, with only his own courage for company. I am still alive only because I long to see him come back.
elementary: A brave soldier leaves home to win a great contest, taking only his courage with him. His wife at home is very sad, but one thing keeps her going: the hope of seeing him walk back through the door. That hope is like a lamp that keeps her heart from going dark.
university: The couplet balances two desires with the same verb, nacai (‘longing’, here in the old verbal form nacaii): he left out of uraṉ nacai, desire for strength or victory, with uḷḷam tuṇaiyāka, his own spirit as his only companion; she lives on out of varal nacai, desire for his return. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss uraṉ as victory (வெற்றி) and uḷḷam as zeal (ஊக்கம்); Solomon Pappaiah adds a note of reproach, reading that he spurned her companionship to make his resolve his companion. Iṉṉum uḷēṉ, ‘I still exist’, implies that only this hope keeps her alive, a recurring motif in the kaṟpu section. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கூடிய காமம் பிரிந்தார் வரவுள்ளிக்
கோடுகொ டேறுமென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Kootiya kaamam pirindhaar varavullik
koaduko daerumen nenju.
current_meaning: Thinking of the return of the one who left, with all the love we shared, my heart climbs from branch to branch to look out for him.
elementary: Have you ever climbed a tree to see far away? The lady in this verse feels so excited thinking her husband might be coming home that it is as if her heart climbs up into the treetops, branch after branch, trying to spot him on the road.
university: The striking image is kōṭu koṭu ēṟum eṉ neñcu, ‘my heart climbs branch upon branch’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it literally as the heart climbing to the treetop to watch the road; Sivayogi Sivakumar compares it to a creeper that outgrows the pole it climbs; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as the heart, freed of sorrow, spreading branches and growing upward in joy, which is close to Pope’s ‘my heart with rapture swells’. Kūṭiya kāmam pirintār, ‘he who parted from the love we had joined in’, recalls their earlier union. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar takes the couplet as the heroine’s eager anticipation at news or thought of his coming. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காண்கமன் கொண்கனைக் கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின்
நீங்கும்என் மென்தோள் பசப்பு.
transliteration:
Kaankaman konkanaik kannaarak kandapin
neengum-en men-dhoal pasappu.
current_meaning: Let me just see my husband until my eyes are full. Once I have seen him, the paleness on my soft arms will go away by itself.
elementary: When you are missing someone, you can feel pale and tired. But the moment you see them, you feel better right away. The lady in this verse says: “I just need to see him properly, and all my paleness will disappear like magic.”
university: Kāṇka maṉ is an optative: ‘may I see’, with maṉ marking an intense wish. Koṇkaṉ, ‘husband’ (originally ‘lord of the seashore’ in the neytal landscape), is to be seen kaṇṇāra, ‘to the eyes’ full’. Pacappu is pacalai, the sallow pallor that in Tamil love convention spreads over a woman’s body in separation; chapter 119 is devoted to it. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say it will vanish ‘of itself’ (தானே) once she sees him, so the cure is sight alone. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar treats this as her answer to the friend who urges patience. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வருகமன் கொண்கன் ஒருநாள் பருகுவன்
பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட.
transliteration:
Varukaman kon-kan oru-naal parukuvan
paidhalnhoi ellaam keda.
current_meaning: Let my husband come back, even for one day. I will drink in his love until all this sickness of sorrow is gone.
elementary: When you are very thirsty, a cool drink makes you feel better all over. The lady says being with her husband again would be like that: after missing him for so long, being with him would wash away all her sadness.
university: Again an optative: varuka maṉ, ‘may he come’, with oru nāḷ, ‘even one day’, suggesting that a single day would suffice. Parukuvaṉ, ‘I shall drink’, is the chapter’s boldest metaphor: she will take in his presence as one drinks to slake thirst (Pope: ‘I’ll drink that nectar’), so that paital nōy, the anguished sickness of separation, is wholly destroyed (ellām keṭa). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss parukuvaṉ as ‘enjoy fully’ (நுகர்வேன்), and Puliyur Kesikan as ‘drink in delight’ (இன்பத்தை பருகுவேன்). The image belongs to the conventions of akam poetry and should be read as the delight of reunion. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்
கண்அன்ன கேளிர் விரன்.
transliteration:
Pulappaen-kol pulluvaen kolloa kalappaenkol
kan-anna kaelir viran.
current_meaning: When he comes back, he who is as dear to me as my own eyes, should I sulk, or hug him, or do both? I cannot decide.
elementary: Imagine your best friend went away for a long time without visiting. When they finally come back, part of you wants to say “Hmph, where were you?” and part of you wants to give them a big hug. The lady in this verse feels both at once, and she just can’t decide which to do first.
university: Three rhetorical questions, each with the doubt particle kol: pulappēṉ (shall I show pulavi, the lover’s feigned sulk), pulluvēṉ (shall I embrace), kalappēṉ (shall I mingle the two, or simply unite). Kaṇ aṉṉa kēḷir, ‘the beloved who is like my eyes’, and viraṉ (‘should he come’) set the scene. Solomon Pappaiah reads kalappēṉ as ‘doing both together’ and Kalaignar adds that she is too overwhelmed even to know; the couplet anticipates the later chapters on ūṭal (lovers’ quarrel, chapters 131-133). Textual note: ytamizh.com’s ‘English Couplet’ slot for 1267 contains a prose explanation, and its ‘Couplet Explanation’ (‘This malady (of lust) is manured by the talk of women…’) belongs to Kural 1147, not this couplet. The Tamil text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன் மனைகலந்து
மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து.
transliteration:
Vinaikalandhu vendreeka vaendhan manaikalandhu
maalai ayarkam virundhu.
current_meaning: Let the king fight on and win the war. Then I will join my wife at home, and we will have a feast together this evening.
elementary: Now the husband speaks. He is far away helping the king in a big contest. He thinks: “Let us finish this job and win, and then I can rush home and have a happy dinner with my wife tonight.” He misses her just as much as she misses him.
university: Here the speaker changes: it is the husband, serving with the king (vēntaṉ) on campaign, who voices his own vitumpal, which is why the chapter is ‘mutual’. Viṉai kalantu veṉṟīka, ‘may [the king] engage in the task and win’, is followed by maṉai kalantu, ‘joining my home (wife)’, and mālai ayarkam viruntu, ‘we shall hold a feast in the evening’. The parallel kalantu…kalantu sets the king’s battle beside the husband’s reunion. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the hero’s eagerness for victory as eagerness to be home; Puliyur Kesikan specifies ‘with her in the evening’. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும்சேண் சென்றார்
வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்கு பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Orunaal ezhunaalpoal sellumsaen sendraar
varunaal-vaiththu aengu pavarkku.
current_meaning: For those who long for the day their faraway love will come back, one day drags by as slowly as seven days.
elementary: Do you remember waiting for your birthday or a holiday? The last few days feel sooo long! The verse says that when you are waiting for someone you love to come home, one day can feel as long as a whole week.
university: A general maxim (note the plural ēṅkupavarkku, ‘for those who pine’) caps the chapter’s experience: oru nāḷ eḻu nāḷ pōl cellum, ‘one day passes like seven’, for those who have fixed in mind (vaittu) the day (varu nāḷ) of return of one who has gone far (cēṇ ceṉṟār). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the seven; Solomon Pappaiah generalises to ‘many days’; Kalaignar heightens it to ‘each day like an age (yugam)’. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar takes it as spoken by the heroine of herself, generalised into a truth. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெறின்என்னாம் பெற்றக்கால் என்னாம் உறினென்னாம்
உள்ளம் உடைந்துக்கக் கால்.
transliteration:
Perin-ennaam petrakkaal ennaam urinennaam
ullam udaindhukkak kaal.
current_meaning: If her heart breaks with sorrow and she dies, what good will it be that she gets me back, or has me, or even holds me close?
elementary: The husband worries: “If I stay away too long, she might become so sad that her heart breaks. Then what good would it be to come home? I must hurry back while there is still time.” It is like a promise that is only worth something if you keep it in time.
university: Most commentators, following the tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, give this closing couplet to the husband, who fears for his wife: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘if her heart breaks… what use is it that she gets me?’, and Pope translates ‘If she heart-broken lie, with all her life poured forth’. The triple question peṟiṉ eṉ ām / peṟṟakkāl eṉ ām / uṟiṉ eṉ ām moves from ‘should she obtain [me]’ to ‘having obtained’ to ‘having embraced’, and uḷḷam uṭaintu ukkakkāl means ‘when the heart has broken and spilled away’, a euphemism for dying of grief. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the first person plural (நம்மை) and Kalaignar a neutral ‘each other’, so the speaker is not unanimous, but the sense of urgency is shared. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கரப்பினுங் கையிகந் தொல்லாநின் உண்கண்
உரைக்கல் உறுவதொன் றுண்டு.
transliteration:
Karappinung kaiyikan thollaanin unkan
uraikkal uruvadhon rundu.
current_meaning: Even though you try to hide it, your eyes, darkened with eye makeup, will not stay quiet. They have something to tell me.
elementary: Imagine a friend who says ‘I’m fine’ but whose eyes look sad. You can tell something is wrong, because eyes often say what words keep hidden. The poet says love works the same way: the eyes give away the secret.
university: The chapter title kuṟippaṟivuṟuttal means ‘making known by signs’ (kuṟippu, a hint or covert sign; aṟivuṟuttal, causing to be known), and it belongs to the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, where partners communicate feelings about separation without open speech. Here the husband addresses his wife: karappiṉum (‘though you hide it’), her uṇkaṇ (eyes darkened with collyrium) kai ikantu ollā (‘will not stay within bounds’) and are about to utter (uraikkal uṟuvatu) one thing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as a message the eyes force past her concealment; Solomon Pappaiah stresses the painted eyes; Kalaignar names the hidden message as a love that does not want separation, which fits the chapter’s setting of an impending departure. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi as கையிகந் தொல்லாநின்).

tamil:
கண்ணிறைந்த காரிகைக் காம்பேர்தோட் பேதைக்குப்
பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது.
transliteration:
Kanniraindha kaarikaik kaamperdhot pedhaikkup
penniraindha neermai peridhu.
current_meaning: My innocent love, whose beauty fills my eyes and whose shoulders are smooth like bamboo, has a womanly shyness that is even greater than her beauty.
elementary: Some people are beautiful to look at, but what makes them special is how gentle and kind they are. The poet says his beloved is lovely, but her quiet, modest nature is even bigger than her beauty.
university: The speaker praises the heroine’s kārikai (beauty) that fills the eye (kaṇ niṟainta) and her shoulders like the bamboo (kāmpu ēr tōḷ), a stock Tamil image of smooth, rounded grace; pētai here means an artless, innocent young woman. Her peṇ niṟainta nīrmai (‘a nature full of womanliness’) is said to be peritu, very great. Commentators gloss peṇmai variously: Mu. Varadarasanar as the quality of womanhood, Solomon Pappaiah as an excellence surpassing that found in all women, and Kalaignar as womanliness that is itself her greatest beauty. In the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the speaker is the husband telling the confidante (tōḻi) that his wife’s modesty is so great that she cannot voice her own feelings, which is why they must be read through signs. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்போல் மடந்தை
அணியில் திகழ்வதொன்று உண்டு.
transliteration:
Maniyil thikazhdharu noolpol madandhai
aniyil thikazhvadhondru undu.
current_meaning: Just as the thread shows through the clear beads strung on it, something shines through this young woman's beauty.
elementary: If you thread clear glass beads on a string, you can see the string running through them. The poet says his beloved’s beauty is like those beads: you can see a hidden feeling running through it, if you look closely.
university: The image is of a string of maṇi (gems or crystal beads) through which the nūl (thread) can be seen; the maṭantai (young woman) has something that likewise tikaḻvatu, shines through her aṇi (beauty or adornment). Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss that ‘something’ as a kuṟippu, a hidden intent visible within her beauty; Solomon Pappaiah takes the gems as clear crystal (paḷiṅku) through which the thread is seen, and Kalaignar as a sign that enchants the speaker. In the traditional arrangement the husband speaks to the confidante, saying the wife’s hidden feeling is legible through her looks. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the thread-and-gem simile is also famous from Bhagavad Gita 7.7, though there it describes the divine as the string on which the world is threaded.

tamil:
முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்போல் பேதை
நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன் றுண்டு.
transliteration:
Mukaimokkul ulladhu naatrampol pedhai
nakaimokkul ulladhon rundu.
current_meaning: Just as a sweet smell is hidden inside a flower bud that has not opened, something is hidden inside this innocent girl's small, shy smile.
elementary: A flower bud doesn’t smell much yet, but the sweet smell is already inside, waiting. The poet says his beloved’s small smile is like that bud: it holds a feeling she hasn’t said out loud yet.
university: The couplet pairs two ‘buds’: mukai-mokkuḷ, the closed bud of a flower that holds its nāṟṟam (fragrance), and nakai-mokkuḷ, the bud of a smile, the half-formed smile of the pētai (innocent young woman), which holds ‘something’. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss that something as a kuṟippu, a hidden intent; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar make it explicit as her thoughts of her lover filling the smile. As in 1272-1273, the speaker is traditionally the husband addressing the confidante about signs he can read in the heroine. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; Pope’s rendering on ytamizh (‘budding smile of this dear damsel’s eyes’) adds the eyes, which are not in the Tamil.

tamil:
செறிதொடி செய்திறந்த கள்ளம் உறுதுயர்
தீர்க்கும் மருந்தொன்று உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seridhodi seydhirandha kallam urudhuyar
theerkkum marundhondru udaiththu.
current_meaning: As she left, my love with the tight bangles gave me a secret sign. That sign holds a medicine that cures my deep sorrow.
elementary: Sometimes a friend gives you a small wink or a smile that only you understand, and it makes you feel better right away. The poet says the secret look his beloved gave him was like medicine for his sadness.
university: The heroine is named by her ceṟi toṭi (closely set bangles), and what she did and left behind (ceytu iṟanta) is a kaḷḷam, a stealthy or covert sign. That sign holds one maruntu (medicine) that cures uṟu tuyar, great sorrow. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read kaḷḷam as a covert sign; Solomon Pappaiah stresses that it was shown so that only he would understand it; Kalaignar makes it her mischievous glance. The traditional reading has the husband, anxious about her reaction to his journey, comforted by a hidden sign of her consent or reassurance. Both sites give the same text; ytamizh’s English explanation (‘The well-meant departure of her whose bangles are tight-fitting...’) is a loose rendering of ceytu iṟanta, while Pope’s couplet calls the sign ‘secret wiles’.

tamil:
பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல் அரிதாற்றி
அன்பின்மை சூழ்வ துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Peridhaatrip petpak kalaththal aridhaatri
anpinmai soozhva thudaiththu.
current_meaning: He hugs me with great love and joy. But this hints that he is about to do the hard thing again and leave me, without caring how I feel.
elementary: Imagine a parent who gives you an extra-long hug at the door, and you suddenly realise they are about to go on a trip. The heroine notices her husband’s extra-loving embrace and guesses that he is getting ready to leave her again.
university: The wife, speaking to her confidante, reads her husband’s unusually tender union (peritu āṟṟi, ‘showing great love’; peṭpak kalattal, ‘uniting so as to delight’) as a kuṟippu of something else: aritu āṟṟi, doing the hard thing, separation, and anpiṉmai cūḻvatu, contemplating lovelessness. Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it this way, as does Kalaignar, who says the embrace seems to signal another parting. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first half differently, as her having endured the past separation, so that his present embrace makes her think of his lack of love. Pope’s couplet on ytamizh (‘While lovingly embracing me, his heart is only grieved’) follows the separation reading. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தண்ணந் துறைவன் தணந்தமை நம்மினும்
முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை.
transliteration:
Thannan thuraivan thanandhamai namminum
munnam unarndha valai.
current_meaning: My bangles knew before I did that my husband, the lord of the cool seashore, had left me.
elementary: Sometimes your body knows you are sad before your mind does, like when you lose your appetite. The heroine says her arms grew so thin from missing her husband that her bangles slipped off, even before she understood he had left her in his heart.
university: The husband is called taṇṇam tuṟaivaṉ, ‘lord of the cool shore’, the conventional epithet of the hero of the neytal (seashore) landscape, whose mood in classical Tamil poetics is anxious waiting. His taṇantamai (having parted) was sensed by her vaḷai (bangles) even before (muṉṉam) by herself. The image rests on a classical convention: grief at separation makes the wife’s arms grow thin, so her bangles slip. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as the bangles loosening at his departure; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it, saying he had parted in mind while still with her in body, and her bangles knew it first. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார்எம் காதலர் யாமும்
எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து.
transliteration:
Nerunatruch chendraarem kaadhalar yaamum
ezhunaalem meni pasandhu.
current_meaning: My love left only yesterday, yet my body has turned pale as if seven days had passed.
elementary: When someone you love goes away, even one day can feel like a whole week. The heroine says her husband left just yesterday, but she already looks as tired and pale as if he had been gone seven days.
university: The wife tells her confidante that her kātalar (beloved) left only neṟunaṟṟu (yesterday), yet she is like one parted for eḻu nāḷ (seven days), her mēṉi (body, complexion) pacantu, turned pale with pacalai, the sallow pallor that classical Tamil love poetry treats as the visible sign of separation. All four commentators on both sites agree on the sense; Kalaignar loosens ‘seven days’ to ‘many days’. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The pallor here is itself one of the chapter’s ‘signs’, read on the body rather than in speech.

tamil:
தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி அடிநோக்கி
அஃதாண் டவள்செய் தது.
transliteration:
Thodinokki mendholum nokki adinokki
ahdhaandaval seydhadhu.
current_meaning: She looked at her bangles, looked at her soft shoulders, and looked at her feet. That is what she did there.
elementary: Without saying a word, the girl looks at her bangles, then her arms, then her feet. Her friend explains what she means: ‘If you leave, I will grow thin and my bangles will slip off, so I’d rather walk with you.’ Her looks said it all.
university: This couplet is a pure kuṟippu: three looks, at her toṭi (bangles), her meṉ tōḷ (soft shoulders) and her aṭi (feet), with the comment ‘that is what she did there’ (aḵtu āṇṭu avaḷ ceytatu). It is traditionally spoken by the confidante to the hero, explaining the heroine’s silent gestures. Varadarasanar and Kesikan identify the sign as uṭaṉpōkku, her resolve to go with him on his journey; Solomon Pappaiah spells out the logic: the bangles will slip and the shoulders waste if he leaves her, and her looking at her feet means she will walk with him. Kalaignar reads it the same way. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, which print the āytam form அஃதாண் டவள்.

tamil:
பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்தென்ப கண்ணினால்
காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு.
transliteration:
Penninaal penmai udaiththenpa kanninaal
kaamanoi solli iravu.
current_meaning: People say that to show the pain of love with your eyes, and so to plead with the one you love, is the most womanly thing a woman can do.
elementary: Sometimes the bravest thing a shy person can do is to show with their eyes how much they need someone, without saying it out loud. The poet says that this gentle, silent asking is the finest kind of grace.
university: The couplet generalises the chapter: kaṇṇiṉāl kāma nōy colli iravu, ‘telling the sickness of love with the eyes and entreating’, is said (eṉpa, ‘they say’) to be peṇmai, womanliness, added to womanliness (peṇṇiṉāl peṇmai uṭaittu). Varadarasanar and Kesikan specify the entreaty as asking the husband not to leave; Kalaignar makes it a plea to be taken along, linking it to 1279’s udanpokku; Solomon Pappaiah frames it as asking that the love-sickness be cured. Pope renders the sense as ‘womanhood’s most womanly device’. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; its framing assumes the classical ideal that a woman should not declare love in words, which modern readers may note as a convention of its time.

tamil:
உள்ளக் களித்தலும் காண மகிழ்தலும்
கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற் குண்டு.
transliteration:
Ullak kaliththalum kaana makizhdhalum
kallukkil kaamaththir kundu.
current_meaning: To feel joy just by thinking of someone, and to be happy just by seeing them: strong drink cannot do this, but love can.
elementary: A treat only makes you happy once you eat it. But when you miss someone you love, just thinking of them makes you smile, and seeing them makes you jump for joy. The poet says love is stronger than any treat, because it works even before it arrives.
university: The chapter title puṇarcci vitumpal combines puṇarcci (union, coming together) and vitumpal (eager longing, impatient haste); it belongs to the kaṟpu (wedded love) section and follows kuṟippaṟivuṟuttal, describing the eagerness of husband and wife to be reunited, an eagerness strong enough to override the playful sulking (ūṭal) that convention expects. The couplet contrasts kaḷ (toddy, palm wine) with kāmam (love): uḷḷak kaḷittal is intoxication from mere thought (uḷḷal, to think) and kāṇa makiḻtal is joy from mere sight, and neither belongs to wine, which must actually be drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as two states (nilai) that wine lacks but love possesses; Solomon Pappaiah adds that thought excites without overwhelming the senses while sight overwhelms them; Kalaignar sums it up as ‘wine gives pleasure only when drunk, love gives it at a thought or a glance.’ The comparison with wine recurs in kural 1288 of this chapter and echoes the earlier chapter on abstaining from toddy (kaḷḷuṇṇāmai, ch. 93). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும் பனைத்துணையும்
காமம் நிறைய வரின்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyum oodaamai vaendum panaiththunaiyum
kaamam niraiya varin.
current_meaning: When love comes in full, as tall as a palm tree, you should not sulk even as much as a tiny grain of millet.
elementary: If you have a mountain of love for someone, it makes no sense to stay grumpy with them over a crumb-sized thing. The poet compares the love to a tall palm tree and the grumpiness to a tiny seed.
university: The couplet sets two proverbial Tamil measures against each other: tiṉai (Italian millet, the smallest grain) and paṉai (the palmyra palm, the tallest tree), each with tuṇai (‘measure, extent’). When kāmam comes niṟaiya (‘in fullness’) to the measure of a palmyra, one should not engage in ūṭal (lovers’ feigned sulking) even to the measure of a millet seed. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as general advice, while Solomon Pappaiah applies it specifically to the wife and her husband; in the traditional reading the heroine says this when her companion suggests she show displeasure at her husband’s long absence. Ūṭal is otherwise a valued convention of akam poetry (the final chapters 130-133 are devoted to it), so the couplet’s point is that eagerness for reunion overrides it here. Pope’s translation (‘Distrust can find no place small as the millet grain’) renders ūṭal loosely as distrust. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும் கொண்கனைக்
காணா தமையல கண்.
transliteration:
Paenaadhu petpavae seyyinum konkanaik
kaanaa thamaiyala kan.
current_meaning: Even if my husband ignores me and does only what he likes, my eyes cannot rest without seeing him.
elementary: Sometimes a friend ignores you, and you feel hurt, but you still keep looking out for them at the window. The wife in this poem feels the same: even when her husband seems careless, her eyes keep searching for him.
university: Pēṇātu means ‘without caring for (me)’, ‘neglecting’, and peṭpavē ceyyiṉum ‘even if he does only what he desires’; koṇkaṉ (‘husband, the one who took me’) is the object of kāṇātu (‘without seeing’), and amaiyala kaṇ ‘the eyes do not rest/settle’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘my eyes do not settle without seeing my lover’, Puliyur Kesikan ‘my eyes find no peace’, and Kalaignar ‘though he does not embrace me and does what pleases him, my eyes are not at peace without seeing him’. The couplet shows the heroine’s will to resent overruled by her eyes’ longing, a motif that links to chapter 118 (kaṇvitumpaḻital, the eyes’ eager suffering). Pope’s prose explanation (‘Though my eyes disregard me and do what is pleasing to my husband’) takes the eyes as the subject of the first clause, a construal not followed by the modern commentators cited here. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் தோழி அதுமறந்து
கூடற்கண் சென்றதுஎன் னெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ootarkan sendraenman thoazhi adhumarandhu
koodarkan sendradhuen nenju.
current_meaning: My friend, I went to him meaning to sulk. But my heart forgot all that and went straight to making up with him.
elementary: Imagine planning to stay cross with a friend who came back late from a trip, but the moment you see them you forget and run to hug them. That is what happens to the wife in this poem: her plan to be cross melts away.
university: The heroine addresses her companion (tōḻi): ūṭaṟkaṇ ceṉṟēṉ maṉ, ‘I did go toward sulking’, where the particle maṉ marks a past intention that came to nothing; but atu maṟantu, ‘forgetting it’, eṉ neñcu (‘my heart’) went kūṭaṟkaṇ, ‘toward union’. The neat opposition of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking) and kūṭal (coming together) carries the chapter’s theme: eagerness for reunion overruling the convention of feigned displeasure. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it this way; Solomon Pappaiah specifies that she planned to sulk over his fault before seeing him and forgot it once she saw him; Kalaignar generalises it as the special nature of love. The heart acting apart from the speaker’s will anticipates the next chapter, neñcoṭu pulattal (‘quarrelling with one’s heart’). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்ணேபோல் கொண்கன்
பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து.
transliteration:
Ezhudhungaal koalkaanaak kannaepoal konkan
pazhikaanaen kanda idaththu.
current_meaning: Just as the eye cannot see the brush that puts dark eye makeup on it, I cannot see my husband's faults at the moment I see him.
elementary: Your eye can see everything around it, but it cannot see the little brush that touches it when someone puts on eyeliner, because it is too close. The wife says her husband’s faults are like that brush: when he is right in front of her, she cannot see them.
university: The simile draws on the practice of applying mai (collyrium, kohl) with a slender rod (kōl): eḻutuṅkāl, ‘while painting/applying’, the eye does not see the kōl, though it saw it a moment earlier. So too, kaṇṭa iṭattu (‘at the place/time of seeing him’), she does not see the paḻi (fault, blame) of her koṇkaṉ (husband). Solomon Pappaiah makes the comparison exact: the eye saw the rod before but not while it paints; she brooded on his fault in his absence but cannot see it in his presence. Kalaignar names the fault as his having left her. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow the same line. The domestic, almost tactile image is characteristic of the Kural’s Inbam section, and the couplet pairs closely with the next (1286). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால்
காணேன் தவறல் லவை.
transliteration:
Kaanungaal kaanaen thavaraaya kaanaakkaal
kaanaen thavaral lavai.
current_meaning: When I see him, I see none of his faults. When I do not see him, I see nothing but his faults.
elementary: When your best friend is with you, you only remember how fun they are. When they are away and forgot to call, you can only think of what they did wrong. The wife in this poem notices she does exactly this with her husband.
university: The couplet is built on a chiasmus of kāṇ- (‘see’): kāṇuṅkāl kāṇēṉ tavaṟāya (‘when I see [him], I do not see what is wrong’), kāṇākkāl kāṇēṉ tavaṟu allavai (‘when I do not see [him], I do not see what is not wrong’). The wordplay turns on two senses of seeing, physical sight of the husband and mental perception of faults. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as ‘I do not see the good things that are not faults’; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as ‘I see nothing but faults’. The couplet extends the previous one (1285) by adding the opposite case and so explains why the heroine plans to sulk in absence yet forgets it in presence (1284). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi as தவறல் லவை).

tamil:
உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய் பவரேபோல்
பொய்த்தல் அறிந்தென் புலந்து.
transliteration:
Uyththal arindhu punalpaai pavaraepoal
poiththal arindhen pulandhu.
current_meaning: I am like people who jump into a flood knowing it will sweep them away. What is the use of sulking when I know it will not work?
elementary: If you know the river is too strong and will carry you off, it is silly to jump in. The wife says staying cross with her husband is like that: she knows her anger will be swept away the moment she sees him, so why even try?
university: Uyttal means ‘carrying off, sweeping away’ (of a current), and puṉal pāyvar are ‘those who leap into the flood’; poyttal is ‘failing, proving false’, and pulantu ‘having sulked’. The last word eṉ is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the interrogative ‘what (use)?’, giving ‘what is gained by sulking, knowing it will fail?’, with Pappaiah specifying that her anger cannot succeed. The Sivayogi Sivakumar gloss on ytamizh instead reads eṉ as ‘I’ (‘knowing it will come to nothing, I sulk’), and Pope’s couplet likewise renders it as a confession (‘So did I anger feign’), so the line can be read as a rhetorical question or as a rueful admission. The flood simile expresses the overwhelming force of the desire for reunion that the chapter describes. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும் களித்தார்க்குக்
கள்ளற்றே கள்வநின் மார்பு.
transliteration:
Iliththakka innaa seyinum kaliththaarkkuk
kallatrae kalvanin maarbu.
current_meaning: You thief! Even though you do hurtful, shameful things to me, your chest draws me the way strong drink draws someone who craves it.
elementary: Some people keep going back to something even when it is bad for them, because they just can’t resist it. The wife playfully calls her husband a ‘thief’ who stole her heart: even when he hurts her by being away, she can’t stop wanting to be close to him.
university: The wife addresses her husband as kaḷva (‘thief’, a term of endearment for one who has stolen her heart, with a hint of reproach). Iḷittakka iṉṉā ceyiṉum means ‘though it does painful things fit to bring disgrace’; kaḷittārkku kaḷ aṟṟē, ‘like toddy to those who have revelled in it’; niṉ mārpu, ‘your breast’, i.e. his embrace. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as toddy that, despite the shame it brings, makes drinkers crave it more and more; Kalaignar renders kaḷva as ‘thief who stole my heart’; Solomon Pappaiah uses ‘deceiver’ and adds that the husband reads her thoughts in her glance and comforts her, a bridge to 1290. The wine comparison returns from 1281 but now stresses compulsive attraction despite harm, recalling the ruinous drinker of chapter 93. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம் சிலர்அதன்
செவ்வி தலைப்படு வார்.
transliteration:
Malarinum mellidhu kaamam silaradhan
sevvi thalaippadu vaar.
current_meaning: Love is softer than a flower. Only a few people know how to enjoy it at its very best.
elementary: A flower petal is so soft that if you squeeze it, it gets crushed. The poet says love is even softer than that, so you must be gentle and patient with it. Not many people learn how to care for it properly.
university: Malariṉum melliti kāmam: ‘love (kāmam) is softer/more delicate than a flower’. Puliyur Kesikan specifies the flower as aṉiccam, the proverbially delicate flower that withers even at a breath (cf. kural 90 and 1111). Cevvi means ‘ripeness, right moment, perfection’ and talaippaṭuvār ‘those who attain/grasp’; so few attain love’s cevvi. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘few know this truth and obtain its good fruit’; Solomon Pappaiah stresses having the right place, time and circumstances; Kalaignar ‘few enjoy it with the same delicacy’. The couplet is often quoted independently as the Kural’s most celebrated statement on love, and here it explains why both partners must set aside sulking: a love so delicate is easily bruised. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh joins சிலர்அதன்).

tamil:
கண்ணின் துனித்தே கலங்கினாள் புல்லுதல்
என்னினும் தான்விதுப் புற்று.
transliteration:
Kannin thuniththae kalanginaal pulludhal
enninum thaanvidhup putru.
current_meaning: She showed she was upset only with her eyes. Then, wanting the hug even more than I did, she melted into my arms.
elementary: Have you ever tried to look cross at someone you missed, only to break into a smile and give them a hug first? The husband in this poem says his wife did just that: her eyes looked upset, but she was quicker than him to hug.
university: Here the husband speaks, recalling a meeting: kaṇṇiṉ tuṉittē, ‘sulking (tuṉi, displeasure) only by/with the eyes’; kalaṅkiṉāḷ, ‘she was stirred, melted’; pullutal eṉṉiṉum tāṉ vituppuṟṟu, ‘she being more eager (vitumpu, the root of the chapter title) than I to embrace’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss that she sulked only as far as a glance, and then, wanting the embrace more eagerly than he did, forgot her displeasure and came into his arms; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read the same. The Sivayogi Sivakumar gloss on ytamizh takes kalaṅkiṉāḷ more literally as her eyes clouding with tears. By ending with the husband’s voice, the chapter confirms that the eagerness for reunion was mutual and that it overcame the convention of ūṭal on both sides. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல் கண்டும் எவன்நெஞ்சே
நீஎமக்கு ஆகா தது.
transliteration:
Avarnenju avarkkaadhal kandum evannenjae
nee-emakku aakaa thadhu.
current_meaning: My heart, you have seen how his heart stays on his side alone. So why do you not stay on my side?
elementary: Imagine two friends on a team. One friend’s helper always sticks by him, but your own helper keeps running over to the other side. You would ask, ‘Why aren’t you on my side?’ The wife in this poem asks her own heart that same question.
university: The chapter title neñcoṭu pulattal means ‘sulking with (one’s own) heart’: in the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, the husband has returned, the wife wishes to stage a lovers’ quarrel (ūṭal/pulavi) over his long absence, but her heart refuses to cooperate and rushes toward him, so she turns her reproach on the heart itself. Here she observes that avar neñcu avarkku ātal (‘his heart being his own’, i.e. siding with him and not thinking of her) is plain to see, yet her heart (neñcē) will not be emakku (‘ours’, on her side). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read ātal as ‘becoming a companion/ally (tuṇai)’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar add that her heart keeps melting toward him instead; Pope renders it ‘You see his heart is his alone; O heart, why not be all my own?’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the chapter title is printed நெஞ்சொடுபுலத்தல் on ytamizh and நெஞ்சோடு புலத்தல் on thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறாஅ தவர்க்கண்ட கண்ணும் அவரைச்
செறாஅரெனச் சேறியென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Uraaa thavarkkanda kannum avaraich
cheraa-arenach chaeriyen nenju.
current_meaning: My heart, even after seeing that he does not care for me, you still go to him, thinking he will not be angry.
elementary: Think of a puppy that keeps running to someone who ignores it, wagging its tail and hoping for a pat. The puppy does not stop to think. The wife says her heart is like that puppy: it runs to her husband even when he has not shown much love.
university: Uṟāatavar is ‘one who does not draw near’, i.e. who shows no love (uṟu, to approach, be attached); ceṟāar is ‘he will not be angry’, and cēṟi ‘you go’. Both uṟāa and ceṟāa show the long-vowel extension (aḷapeṭai) used for metre, also seen in 1295. The commentators agree on the sense: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan have the heart go to the beloved ‘thinking he will not hate us’, and Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘thinking he will not be angry if we go’; Pope renders ‘Why go to him as though he were not enemy?’ The point within the chapter is that the heart’s eagerness undercuts the wife’s plan to sulk. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the same text.

tamil:
கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார்இல் என்பதோ நெஞ்சேநீ
பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்.
transliteration:
Kettaarkku nattaar-il enpadho nenjaenee
pettaangu avarpin selal.
current_meaning: My heart, is it because "people in trouble have no friends" that you leave me and follow him as you please?
elementary: There is an old saying that when someone is in trouble, their friends disappear. The wife feels sad and alone, and even her own heart has left her to go after her husband. So she asks her heart, ‘Did you leave me because I am having a hard time?’
university: The first line quotes a proverb: keṭṭārkku naṭṭār il, ‘the ruined have no friends’; the wife bitterly applies it to herself, worn down by separation. Peṭṭāṅku means ‘as you please, at your own desire’ and avar piṉ celal ‘going after him’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read keṭṭār as ‘those ruined by suffering’, and Kalaignar puts it as ‘those destroyed by sorrow have no friends to stand by them’; Pope renders ‘The ruined have no friends, they say; and so, my heart, / To follow him, at thy desire, from me thou dost depart.’ The rhetorical question (eṉpatō, ‘is it that…?’) carries the chapter’s tone of affectionate reproach. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இனிஅன்ன நின்னொடு சூழ்வார்யார் நெஞ்சே
துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்காண் மற்று.
transliteration:
Ini-anna ninnodu soozhvaaryaar nenjae
thuniseydhu thuvvaaikaan matru.
current_meaning: My heart, you will not sulk first and then enjoy making up. So who will ever plan such things with you again?
elementary: Imagine you and a friend plan to act a little upset with someone to show your feelings, and then make up. But the moment that person walks in, your friend runs and hugs him. You might say, ‘I’m never planning anything with you again!’ That is what the wife says to her heart.
university: Tuṉi is a strong form of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking), and tuvvāy means ‘you will not enjoy’; the commentators read the line as ‘you will not first sulk and then enjoy (the reunion that follows)’. In Tamil love poetics the reconciliation after ūṭal is itself a pleasure, which is why the wife complains that her eager heart skips it. Iṉi aṉṉa niṉṉoṭu cūḻvār yār, ‘hereafter who will consult with you about such things?’, is her mock threat to stop taking the heart into her counsels; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar add ‘I will not’. Pope renders ‘See, thou first show offended pride, and then submit, I bade; / Henceforth such council who will share with thee my heart?’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின்பிரிவு அஞ்சும்
அறாஅ இடும்பைத்தென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Peraaamai anjum perinpirivu anjum
araaa idumpaiththen nenju.
current_meaning: When he is away, my heart fears it will not have him. When he is here, it fears he will leave. So my heart is never free from pain.
elementary: Think of a child waiting for a favourite toy: before getting it, she worries she never will, and after getting it, she worries she will lose it. The wife’s heart is like that with her husband: worried when he is gone, and worried when he is home that he will go again.
university: The couplet is built on parallel clauses: peṟāamai añcum (‘it fears not having him’) and peṟiṉ pirivu añcum (‘having him, it fears separation’), leading to aṟāa iṭumpaittu eṉ neñcu, ‘my heart is (a thing) of unceasing distress’. Peṟāamai and aṟāa again show metrical vowel lengthening (aḷapeṭai). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan agree on the reading; Solomon Pappaiah makes the setting explicit, ‘when my husband was away… when he has come’. Pope renders ‘I fear I shall not gain, I fear to lose him when I gain; / And thus my heart endures unceasing pain.’ Within the chapter this explains why the heart cannot afford to sulk: even in his presence it already fears his next departure. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால் என்னைத்
தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Thaniye irundhu ninaiththakkaal ennaith
thiniya irundhadhen nenju.
current_meaning: Whenever I sat alone and thought of him, my own heart seemed ready to eat me alive.
elementary: Have you ever been alone and kept thinking about something sad until you felt worse and worse? Your thoughts can feel like they are gnawing at you. The wife says that when she was alone, her own heart chewed at her like that.
university: Taṉiyē iruntu niṉaittakkāl means ‘when I sat alone and thought’, and tiṉiya iruntatu ‘it was there to eat (me)’: the heart, instead of comforting her, devoured her. Commentators differ on what she was thinking of: Mu. Varadarasanar says ‘his faults’ (avaruṭaiya tavaṟukaḷ), which fits the chapter’s quarrel; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar say ‘the separation from her lover’; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the heart, ‘not being a companion to me’, tormented her. Pope renders ‘My heart consumes me when I ponder lone, / And all my lover’s cruelty bemoan.’ The past tense (iruntatu) recalls the time of separation now that he is back. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாணும் மறந்தேன் அவர்மறக் கல்லாஎன்
மாணா மடநெஞ்சிற் பட்டு.
transliteration:
Naanum marandhaen avarmarak kallaaen
maanaa madanenjir pattu.
current_meaning: My foolish heart has no pride and cannot forget him. Stuck with such a heart, I have even forgotten my shyness.
elementary: Sometimes when we miss someone very much, we do things we would normally feel shy about, like crying in front of others or running to hug them in public. The wife says her heart missed her husband so much that she forgot to be shy.
university: Nāṇ is the feminine modesty or sense of shame that classical Tamil poetics treats as a woman’s guarding virtue; avar maṟakkallā is ‘unable to forget him’, and māṇā maṭa neñcu ‘my undignified, foolish heart’ (māṇā, lacking excellence; maṭam, simplicity/folly). Paṭṭu, ‘having fallen in with’, makes the heart the bad company that led her astray. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan add that nāṇ is ‘something that should not be forgotten’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads the heart as ‘unsteady’ and the husband as one ‘who has forgotten me’. Pope renders ‘Fall’n ’neath the sway of this ignoble foolish heart, / Which will not him forget, I have forgotten shame.’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எள்ளின் இளிவாம்என்று எண்ணி அவர்திறம்
உள்ளும் உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ellin ilivaam-endru enni avarthiram
ullum uyirkkaadhal nenju.
current_meaning: My heart loves him as much as life itself. It thinks that looking down on him would only shame itself, so it keeps thinking of his good points.
elementary: When someone you love lets you down, you might want to say mean things about them. But a loving heart thinks, ‘If I say bad things about him, it makes me look bad too,’ and remembers his good side instead. The wife’s heart does exactly that.
university: Eḷḷiṉ iḷivām means ‘if (I) scorn (him), it will be a disgrace (to me)’; avar tiṟam uḷḷum, ‘it thinks of his qualities (or ways)’. Uyirkkātal neñcu is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as ‘the heart that loves life’ (fearing disgrace as worse than death), while Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar take it as ‘the heart that loves him as its own life’. Commentators also differ on avar tiṟam: ‘his noble qualities’ (Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Kalaignar) versus ‘his coming and our union’ (Pappaiah). Pope renders ‘If I contemn him, then disgrace awaits me evermore; / My soul that seeks to live his virtues numbers o’er.’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
துன்பத்திற்கு யாரே துணையாவார் தாமுடைய
நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி.
transliteration:
Thunpaththirku yaarae thunaiyaavaar thaamudaiya
nenjan thunaiyal vazhi.
current_meaning: When you are in trouble, who will help you, if even your own heart does not?
elementary: When you feel sad, the first one who can comfort you is you: you can tell yourself, ‘It will be okay.’ But if even your own feelings turn against you, who else can help? The wife asks this when her heart will not stand by her.
university: Tuṉpattiṟku yārē tuṇaiyāvār, ‘who indeed will be a companion in sorrow?’, with the emphatic -ē, and tām uṭaiya neñcam tuṇai al vaḻi, ‘when the heart that one owns is not a companion’. Here the wife generalises her complaint into a maxim (the plural tām gives it the force of ‘anyone’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress tām urimaiyākap peṟṟa, ‘that one possesses by right’; Kalaignar reads tuṇai as ‘support to bear’ the sorrow. Pope renders ‘And who will aid me in my hour of grief, / If my own heart comes not to my relief?’ With 1300 this forms the chapter’s closing pair of general sayings. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (thirukkural.net prints நெஞ்சந் with the same sandhi).

tamil:
தஞ்சம் தமரல்லர் ஏதிலார் தாமுடைய
நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி.
transliteration:
Thanjam thamarallar aedhilaar thaamudaiya
nenjam thamaral vazhi.
current_meaning: When your own heart does not act like your family, it is no surprise that strangers do not either.
elementary: If even your own feelings won’t be kind to you, you can’t be surprised when people you hardly know aren’t kind either. The wife says that since her heart has left her, she can hardly blame others for not standing by her.
university: Tañcam here is glossed by the commentators as ‘easy, a slight matter’ (eḷitu): Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read ‘it is easy (natural) for strangers (ētilār) not to be kin (tamar allar) when one’s own heart (tām uṭaiya neñcam) is not kin’. Puliyur Kesikan agrees, calling it ‘natural’ (iyalpāṉatē). Sivayogi Sivakumar instead takes tañcam in its other sense, ‘refuge’: ‘there is no kin to give refuge if one’s own heart is not one’s own’, a variant reading of the same text. Pope renders ‘A trifle is unfriendliness by aliens shown, / When our own heart itself is not our own!’ The couplet closes the chapter by turning the wife’s quarrel into a general truth about the self; it is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
புல்லா திராஅப் புலத்தை அவர்உறும்
அல்லல்நோய் காண்கம் சிறிது.
transliteration:
Pullaa thiraaap pulaththai avar-urum
allalnoai kaankam siridhu.
current_meaning: Hold back your hug and sulk a little. Then we can watch, for a short while, the pain of love that he goes through.
elementary: Imagine a friend comes home very late after promising to be early. Your sister whispers, ‘Pretend to be a tiny bit upset for a minute, so he sees how much he was missed.’ It is a small, gentle game, not real anger, and it only lasts a moment.
university: The chapter on pulavi (a lovers’ sulk within married love, kaṟpu) opens with the speaker, read as the confidante (tōḻi), urging the wife: pullātu irā (‘remain without embracing’) and pulattai (‘sulk’), so that ‘we’ may see (kāṇkam) for a little (ciṟitu) the allal nōy (‘anguished love-sickness’) he will feel. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all gloss it this way, the first-person plural binding the confidante to the wife’s side, and Pope’s verse likewise asks her to stay reserved and decline his proffered love so as to prove his distress a little while. The limiting word ciṟitu anticipates the next couplet’s warning that the sulk must not be prolonged. ytamizh.com prints அவர்உறும் where thirukkural.net prints the joined form அவருறும், a difference of word division only.

tamil:
உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி அதுசிறிது
மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்.
transliteration:
Uppamain thatraal pulavi adhusiridhu
mikkatraal neela vidal.
current_meaning: A little sulking is like the right amount of salt in food. Letting it go on too long is like putting in too much salt.
elementary: A pinch of salt makes soup taste wonderful, but too much salt spoils it. A small, short sulk between people who love each other is like that pinch; a long one ruins everything.
university: The famous image here is culinary: pulavi is uppu amaintaṟṟu (‘like salt properly set’ in food), but to let it lengthen (nīḷa viṭal) is like salt that has become a little excessive (atu ciṟitu mikkaṟṟu). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read ciṟitu with mikku (‘even slightly too much’), stressing how quickly the right measure is lost, while Kalaignar reads the measure as the interval between quarrel (ūṭal) and reunion (kūṭal), and Solomon Pappaiah relates it to the joy of union it is meant to season. The couplet is generally taken as the confidante’s counsel to the wife, balancing the previous verse’s encouragement. Pope renders ‘A cool reserve is like the salt that seasons well the mess, / Too long maintained, ’tis like the salt’s excess.’ ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text.

tamil:
அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்றால் தம்மைப்
புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்.
transliteration:
Alandhaarai allalnoai seydhatraal thammaip
pulandhaaraip pullaa vidal.
current_meaning: Not hugging and making up with the one who is sulking is like adding fresh pain to someone who is already suffering.
elementary: If your little sister is sad and pretending not to talk to you, and you just walk away, she feels even worse than before. A hug at the right moment is what she was secretly waiting for.
university: The address now turns to the husband: to leave unembraced (pullā viṭal) those who have sulked with him (tammaip pulantār) is like inflicting allal nōy (‘anguish, sickness’) on alantār, ‘those already distressed.’ Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss ‘not dispelling the sulk and embracing’ (ūṭal uṇarttit taḻuvāmal), Solomon Pappaiah names the wife explicitly, and Puliyur Kesikan calls such neglect a cruelty; the point is that the sulk is itself a symptom of the pain of separation, so ignoring it compounds that pain. Pope’s explanation reads ‘For men not to embrace those who have feigned dislike is like torturing those already in agony.’ The two web texts agree.

tamil:
ஊடி யவரை உணராமை வாடிய
வள்ளி முதலரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Ooti yavarai unaraamai vaatiya
valli mudhalarin thatru.
current_meaning: Not making up with the one who is sulking is like cutting the root of a vine that is already drooping.
elementary: A thirsty plant droops when it needs water. If, instead of watering it, someone cut its root, it would never recover. Someone who is sulking is like that drooping plant: they need care, not to be ignored.
university: Ūṭiyavarai uṇarāmai, ‘not making those who sulk understand (and so ending the sulk),’ is likened to cutting at the root (mutal arital) a valli creeper that is already wilted (vāṭiya). Uṇartal here is the technical term for appeasing a lover’s sulk by explanation and tenderness; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss ‘without showing love,’ while Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah add that the creeper had already withered for want of water, so the cutting destroys any chance of recovery. The image completes the previous couplet: the sulk is a sign of a love already parched by separation, and neglect kills it outright. Pope renders the explanation ‘Not to reconcile those who have feigned dislike is like cutting a faded creeper at its root.’ The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு ஏஎர் புலத்தகை
பூஅன்ன கண்ணார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Nalaththakai nallavarkku aeer pulaththakai
pooanna kannaar akaththu.
current_meaning: Even for good men with fine qualities, the real beauty is the loving little anger that rises in the hearts of their wives with flower-like eyes.
elementary: A kind, good person is like a fine house. What makes the house feel truly loved is that someone inside cares enough to be a little upset when you are late. That small fuss is a sign of how much you matter.
university: Nalattakai nallavar are ‘good men of excellent quality’; their ēr (‘beauty, ornament’) is the pulattakai (‘the excellence of sulking’) that arises akattu (‘within,’ in the heart) of pū aṉṉa kaṇṇār, ‘those with flower-like eyes.’ The paradox is that the husband’s virtues are crowned not by praise but by his beloved’s pique, which proves her attachment; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it this way, Solomon Pappaiah speaks of the abundance of sulking in the wife’s mind, and Kalaignar says such pique ‘adds beauty’ to noble lovers. Pope translates ‘Even to men of good and worthy mind, the petulance / Of wives with flowery eyes lacks not a lovely grace.’ ytamizh.com divides நல்லவர்க்கு ஏஎர் and பூஅன்ன, while thirukkural.net prints the sandhi forms நல்லவர்க் கேஎர் and பூவன்ன.

tamil:
துனியும் புலவியும் இல்லாயின் காமம்
கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று.
transliteration:
Thuniyum pulaviyum illaayin kaamam
kaniyum karukkaayum atru.
current_meaning: Love without its big quarrels and small sulks is like fruit that is either too ripe or still hard and green.
elementary: A mango that is too soft and mushy is no good, and one that is still hard and green is no good either. Love that never has a single little disagreement is a bit like that: it has lost its just-right sweetness.
university: Two grades of lovers’ anger are named: tuṉi, the grown or deep sulk, and pulavi, the young or light sulk, as Solomon Pappaiah glosses them (vaḷarnta ūṭal and iḷam ūṭal); without them kāmam is like kaṉi (fruit gone too ripe) and karukkāy (fruit not yet ripe). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read both fruits as useless, the over-ripe one past its best and the unripe one inedible, while Kalaignar adds ‘rotten’ to the over-ripe fruit; some readers pair the two terms with the two fruits, but the commentators quoted take the comparison as a whole. Pope’s couplet, ‘Love without hatred is ripened fruit; / Without some lesser strife, fruit immature,’ makes that pairing explicit. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊடலின் உண்டாங்கோர் துன்பம் புணர்வது
நீடுவ தன்றுகொல் என்று.
transliteration:
Oodalin untaangoar thunpam punarvadhu
needuva thandrukol endru.
current_meaning: Even in a lovers' sulk there is a kind of pain: the worry, "Will our time together last long enough?"
elementary: When you pretend to be cross with a friend during a sleepover, part of you worries, ‘What if this wastes our fun time together?’ The game is nice, but it also has a little worry inside it.
university: Ūṭalin uṇṭu āṅku ōr tuṉpam, ‘in sulking too there is a certain sorrow,’ namely the fear, puṇarvatu nīṭuvatu aṉṟu kol, ‘whether union will not last long.’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read nīṭuvatu as ‘prolonging, lasting’: the lovers fear that time lost to sulking shortens their time together. Pope’s verse instead asks ‘Will reunion sweet be long delayed?’, reading the worry as delay of reconciliation rather than brevity of union, and his prose explanation follows the same line; both readings keep the paradox that the sulk, meant to heighten love, carries its own anxiety. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நோதல் எவன்மற்று நொந்தாரென்று அஃதறியும்
காதலர் இல்லா வழி.
transliteration:
Noadhal evanmatru nondhaarendru aqdhariyum
kaadhalar illaa vazhi.
current_meaning: What use is it to feel sad when there is no loved one who will understand, "They are hurting because of me"?
elementary: If you sulk in your room, it only helps if someone who loves you notices and comes to ask what is wrong. If nobody notices at all, the sulking just makes you lonely.
university: Nōtal evaṉ maṟṟu, ‘what then is the use of grieving,’ when there are no kātalar, ‘lovers,’ who know it (aḵtu aṟiyum) as nontār eṉṟu, ‘she has grieved (because of us).’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the lover’s grief as worthwhile only when the beloved recognizes himself as its cause; Kesikan adds that such a lover would then try to remove it. The verse states the precondition of the whole pulavi convention: a sulk is a message, and it needs a receiver. Pope’s prose explanation, ‘What avails sorrow when I am without a wife who can understand the cause of my sorrow?’, puts the words in the husband’s mouth, whereas the Tamil commentators leave the speaker general. ytamizh.com prints நொந்தாரென்று அஃதறியும் and thirukkural.net the sandhi form நொந்தாரென் றஃதறியும்.

tamil:
நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே புலவியும்
வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது.
transliteration:
Neerum nizhaladhu inidhae pulaviyum
veezhunar kannae inidhu.
current_meaning: Water is sweet only when it is in the shade. In the same way, sulking is sweet only with those who truly love you.
elementary: Water in a sunny puddle gets hot and yucky, but water in a cool shady pond tastes lovely. A little sulk is only nice between people who love each other; with someone who does not care, it is just unpleasant.
university: Nīrum niḻalatu iṉitē, ‘even water is sweet only when in the shade,’ and pulaviyum vīḻunar kaṇṇē iṉitu, ‘sulking too is sweet only with (vīḻunar) those who desire/love.’ The emphatic -ē particles stress exclusivity: pique has its charm only inside a secure, mutual love. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss vīḻunar as those who show love; Solomon Pappaiah contrasts water under the sun with water under the shade; Kalaignar notes that water by the shade is cool. Pope renders ‘Water is pleasant in the cooling shade; / So coolness for a time with those we love.’ ytamizh.com divides நிழலது இனிதே, while thirukkural.net prints the metrical division நிழல தினிதே, the same text.

tamil:
ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு என்நெஞ்சம்
கூடுவேம் என்பது அவா.
transliteration:
Oodal unanga viduvaaroadu en-nenjam
kooduvaem enpadhu avaa.
current_meaning: He leaves my sulk to dry up without comforting me, yet my heart still says, "Let us be with him." That is nothing but pure desire.
elementary: Sometimes a friend does not even notice you are upset, and yet you still want to play with them. Your heart just wants to be with them anyway. That is how strong caring can be.
university: Ūṭal uṇaṅka viṭuvār, ‘one who leaves (my) sulk to dry up and wither’ (uṇaṅku, ‘to wither, dry’), without soothing it; that my heart (eṉ neñcam) still says kūṭuvēm, ‘we shall unite,’ with such a person is avā, ‘longing, desire.’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read the wife as speaker, explaining her heart’s persistence as untameable desire, which links the chapter to the preceding one on quarrelling with one’s own heart. Pope’s verse, ‘Of her who leaves me thus in variance languishing,’ and his prose explanation take the husband as speaker; the Tamil itself leaves the gender open. ytamizh.com prints விடுவாரோடு என்நெஞ்சம் … என்பது அவா, and thirukkural.net the sandhi forms விடுவாரோ டென்னெஞ்சம் … என்ப தவா.

tamil:
பெண்ணியலார் எல்லாரும் கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்
நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு.
transliteration:
Penniyalaar ellaarum kannin podhu-unpar
nannen paraththa-nin maarpu
current_meaning: You unfaithful man! All women feast their eyes on your broad chest as if it belongs to everyone. So I will not come near it.
elementary: Imagine your favourite teddy bear being passed around the whole class until it no longer feels like yours. A wife in this poem playfully tells her husband that since everyone admires him, she will pretend she does not want to sit close to him.
university: The chapter title pulavi nuṇukkam means ‘the fine points (nuṇukkam) of love-sulking (pulavi)’: in the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, Valluvar sketches how a loving wife turns the smallest innocent word or act of her husband into a pretext for a mock quarrel, and Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes this first couplet as the wife’s own speech. She addresses him as paratta (‘man of wandering ways’) and says that all of feminine nature (peṇ-iyalār) ‘eat’ his chest with their eyes as a common possession (potu uṇpar), so she will not approach (naṇṇēn) it. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read the eye-feasting literally as other women’s admiring glances, while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it into a charge that he is ‘shared’ with women of the street; Pope renders it ‘From thy regard all womankind enjoys an equal grace; O thou of wandering fickle mind, I shrink from thine embrace.’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊடி இருந்தேமாத் தும்மினார் யாம்தம்மை
நீடுவாழ் கென்பாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Ooti irundhaemaath thumminaar yaamdhammai
neetuvaazh kenpaak karindhu
current_meaning: While I sat sulking, he sneezed. He knew I would have to break my silence and wish him a long life.
elementary: Imagine you are not talking to your brother after a squabble, and he pretends to sneeze so that you will say ‘Bless you!’ without thinking. Now you have spoken, and the game is over. That is the clever trick the husband plays here.
university: This couplet is the wife’s speech (talaivi kūṟṟu): ūṭi iruntēmā means ‘as we were sulking’, and she reports that he sneezed (tummiṉār) knowing (aṟintu) that we would say nīṭu vāḻka (‘live long’) to him. It rests on the old Tamil custom of blessing a person who sneezes, which forces the sulking wife to speak and so end her silence. Solomon Pappaiah adds that he sneezed deliberately and that she, despite herself, did bless him; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it the same way. Pope renders it ‘One day we silent sulked; he sneezed: the reason well I knew; he thought that I, to speak well pleased, would say, “Long life to you!”’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கோட்டுப்பூச் சூடினும் காயும் ஒருத்தியைக்
காட்டிய சூடினீர் என்று.
transliteration:
Koattup-pooch chootinum kaayum oruththiyaik
kaattiya sootineer endru
current_meaning: Even if I wear flowers picked from a tree, she gets angry and says I put them on to show off to some other woman.
elementary: Suppose you wear a new cap to school and your best friend frowns, ‘Who are you trying to impress?’ You only wanted to look nice! The husband here wears flowers and his wife pretends he must be dressing up for someone else.
university: From here the speaker is generally taken to be the husband, reporting the ‘fine points’ of his wife’s sulking. Kōṭṭuppū means flowers that bloom on tree branches (kōṭu), as opposed to creeper or water flowers; even if he wears (cūṭiṉum) such a garland, she grows hot with anger (kāyum), saying ‘you wore them to show (kāṭṭiya) to some woman (oruttiyai)’. Puliyur Kesikan reads the line as the husband putting the flowers on her, while Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take him to be wearing them himself; Pope follows the latter: ‘She cries, “Pray, for what woman now do you put on your flowers?”’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
யாரினும் காதலம் என்றேனா ஊடினாள்
யாரினும் யாரினும் என்று.
transliteration:
Yaarinum kaadhalam endraenaa ootinaal
yaarinum yaarinum endru
current_meaning: When I said, "We love each other more than anyone," she sulked and asked, "More than whom? More than whom?"
elementary: If you tell your friend, ‘You are my best friend, better than all the others,’ a cheeky friend might reply, ‘Which others? Who else is on your list?’ The wife turns her husband’s compliment into a question to tease him.
university: Yāriṉum kātalam means ‘we are lovers beyond anyone’; the husband meant it as the highest praise, but she seizes on yāriṉum (‘than anyone’) as if it implied a list of other women he loves less, and repeats yāriṉum yāriṉum (‘than whom? than whom?’). Solomon Pappaiah spells out her reading: she took him to mean that he loves many and her the most. The humour depends on the comparative form, which presupposes rivals; Kalaignar notes that she ‘misread a natural remark’. Pope renders it ‘“I love you more than all beside,” ’t was thus I gently spoke; “What all, what all?” she instant cried; and all her anger woke.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம் என்றேனாக்
கண்நிறை நீர்கொண் டனள்.
transliteration:
Immaip pirappil piriyalam endraenaak
kannirai neerkon danal
current_meaning: When I said, "We will never be apart in this life," her eyes filled with tears, as if I meant we would part in the next life.
elementary: Imagine telling your grandmother, ‘I will visit you every day this summer!’ and she asks, sadly, ‘Only this summer?’ The wife hears ‘in this life’ and worries it means ‘not in the next one’.
university: Immaip piṟappil means ‘in this present birth’ and piriyalam ‘we shall not part’; the wife takes the limiting phrase to imply that in a later birth (maṟumai) they will part, and her eyes fill (kaṇ niṟai nīr koṇṭaṉaḷ). The couplet assumes the belief in rebirth shared by the Tamil tradition and depends on the idea that true lovers should remain together across births. Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it this way, while Kalaignar has her ask, more sceptically, whether there is a next birth at all. Pope: ‘“While here I live, I leave you not,” I said to calm her fears. She cried, “There, then, I read your thought”; and straight dissolved in tears.’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உள்ளினேன் என்றேன்மற் றென்மறந்தீர் என்றென்னைப்
புல்லாள் புலத்தக் கனள்.
transliteration:
Ullinaen endraen-mat ren-marandheer endrennaip
pullaal pulaththak kanal
current_meaning: When I said, "I thought of you," she asked, "So you had forgotten me?" Then, instead of hugging me, she began to sulk.
elementary: If you tell your friend, ‘I remembered you today!’ a teasing friend might say, ‘Only today? So you forgot me yesterday?’ The wife plays the same word game with her husband.
university: Uḷḷiṉēṉ means ‘I recalled (you)’; the wife argues, as Mu. Varadarasanar puts it, that recalling presupposes forgetting (niṉaippukku muṉ maṟappu uṇṭu), so she asks eṉ maṟantīr (‘why did you forget?’), and, though about to embrace him (pullāḷ, ‘she did not embrace’), turns to sulking (pulattakkaṉaḷ). The logic is the same as in 1314: a loving word is pressed for an implication it never had. Solomon Pappaiah notes that she had begun to embrace him and stopped; Pope: ‘“Each day I called to mind your charms,” “O, then, you had forgot,” she cried, and then her opened arms, forthwith embraced me not.’ The line division reads மற் றென்மறந்தீர் on both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வழுத்தினாள் தும்மினேன் ஆக அழித்தழுதாள்
யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர் என்று.
transliteration:
Vazhuththinaal thumminen aaka azhiththazhudhaal
yaarullith thummineer endru
current_meaning: When I sneezed, she first wished me a long life. Then she took it back and cried, asking, "Who was thinking of you, that you sneezed?"
elementary: Some people say that when you sneeze, someone somewhere is thinking about you. Here the wife first says ‘Bless you!’, then suddenly cries, ‘Wait, who was thinking about you?’
university: The couplet turns on a second Tamil belief about sneezing: that one sneezes when someone is thinking of (uḷḷi) one. She first blesses him (vaḻuttiṉāḷ), as custom requires, then cancels it (aḻittu) and weeps (aḻutāḷ), asking yār uḷḷit tummiṉīr (‘thinking of whom did you sneeze?’, or ‘at whose thought’). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss the blessing as the wish of ‘a hundred years’ (nūṟāṇṭu). Pope: ‘She hailed me when I sneezed one day; but straight with anger seized, she cried; “Who was the woman, pray, thinking of whom you sneezed?”’ The text matches on ytamizh.com (which omits the closing full stop) and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தும்முச் செறுப்ப அழுதாள் நுமர்உள்ளல்
எம்மை மறைத்திரோ என்று.
transliteration:
Thummuch cheruppa azhudhaal numar-ullal
emmai maraiththiroa endru
current_meaning: So I held back my sneeze. Then she cried and said, "Are you hiding from me that your people are thinking of you?"
elementary: Imagine you are told off for sneezing, so next time you hold it in, and then you get told off for hiding it! The poor husband cannot win: sneeze or no sneeze, his wife finds something to pretend-cry about.
university: This couplet is the sequel to 1317: afraid of another quarrel, he suppresses (ceṟuppa) his sneeze (tummu), and she weeps, asking whether he is hiding from us (emmai maṟaittirō) the thought of him held by ‘your people’ (numar uḷḷal). Numar (‘your own ones’) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘those dear to you’ and by Solomon Pappaiah as ‘someone you care for’, a veiled hint at another woman. The two couplets together show the ‘subtlety’ of pulavi: every possible response becomes an occasion for sulking. Pope: ‘And so next time I checked my sneeze; she forthwith wept and cried, (that woman difficult to please), “Your thoughts from me you hide.”’ The wording is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தன்னை உணர்த்தினும் காயும் பிறர்க்கும்நீர்
இந்நீரர் ஆகுதிர் என்று.
transliteration:
Thannai unarththinum kaayum pirarkkum-neer
inneerar aakudhir endru
current_meaning: Even when I comfort her out of her sulk, she gets angry again and says, "So this is how you sweet-talk other women too!"
elementary: Imagine you finally cheer up a grumpy friend with a funny joke, and she says, ‘Hmph, I bet you tell that joke to everyone!’ Even making up becomes a new reason to tease.
university: Taṉṉai uṇarttiṉum means ‘even if I appease her (end her sulk)’; uṇarttal is the technical term for coaxing a lover out of ūṭal. Yet she grows angry (kāyum), saying piṟarkkum nīr innīrar ākutir (‘you must be like this with others too’). Puliyur Kesikan, Mu.
