Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah agree on this reading, and Kalaignar adds that the husband had humbled himself to win her back. The couplet shows pulavi feeding on its own remedy, the reconciliation itself becoming fresh evidence; Pope: ‘I then began to soothe and coax, to calm her jealous mind; “I see,” quoth she, “to other folks how you are wondrous kind.”’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும் அனைத்துநீர்
யாருள்ளி நோக்கினீர் என்று.
transliteration:
Ninaiththirundhu noakkinum kaayum anaiththu-neer
yaarulli noakkineer endru
current_meaning: Even when I just sit and look at her, thinking of her, she gets angry and asks, "Who are you thinking of as you look at me like that?"
elementary: Imagine staring happily at your favourite painting, and your sister asks, ‘Are you comparing it to some other painting?’ The husband just wants to admire his wife, but she pretends he must be comparing her to someone else.
university: Niṉaittiruntu nōkkiṉum means ‘even if I look, having (silently) contemplated’, i.e. gazing at her while dwelling on her beauty; she grows hot (kāyum) and asks yār uḷḷi nōkkiṉīr (‘with whom in mind did you look?’). Aṉaittum is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘all (her features) by comparison’ (ollumaiyāka ellām) and by Solomon Pappaiah as gazing at each of her features, which she takes as matching them against another woman’s. As the chapter’s last couplet it caps the series: speech (1314-1316), sneezing (1317-1318), coaxing (1319), and finally even silent admiration all provoke pulavi. Pope: ‘I silent sat, but thought the more, and gazed on her. Then she cried out, “While thus you eye me o’er, tell me whose form you see.”’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு ஆயினும் ஊடுதல்
வல்லது அவர்அளிக்கு மாறு.
transliteration:
Illai thavaravarkku aayinum ootudhal
Valladhu avaralikku maaru.
current_meaning: Even when he has done nothing wrong, a little sulking can make him show me even more love.
elementary: Sometimes two best friends pretend to be cross for a minute, just so the other one will come and make a fuss over them. Nobody did anything wrong; the little pout simply makes the kindness show. The wife in this poem says a small, pretend quarrel does the same for her husband’s love.
university: The final chapter of the Kural, ūṭal uvakai (‘the joy of lovers’ pique’), turns ūṭal, the feigned or playful sulking of a beloved, from a source of pain in the preceding chapters (pulavi, pulavi nuṇukkam) into a source of delight. Here the wife concedes illai tavaṟu avarkku (‘there is no fault in him’), yet ūṭutal (sulking) is vallatu (‘has the power’) to bring about avar aḷi (his tender grace, aḷi meaning lavish affection). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss the line as ūṭal making him shower greater love on her, and Kalaignar generalises it to lovers on both sides; Pope’s ‘fretful jealousy’ reads the pique more darkly than the Tamil commentators do. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; commentators traditionally assign the opening couplets of the chapter to the wife.

tamil:
ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி நல்லளி
வாடினும் பாடு பெறும்.
transliteration:
Oodalin thoandrum sirudhuni nallali
Vaatinum paadu perum.
current_meaning: The small pain that a lovers' sulk brings may make his kindness droop for a while, but it will come back even stronger.
elementary: A plant that is not watered for one day droops a little, and when you water it again it seems to stand up even taller. A short, small quarrel is like that: love looks a little wilted for a moment, then bounces back stronger.
university: The couplet sets ciṟu tuṉi (‘a small distress’, tuṉi meaning grief or estrangement) arising from ūṭal against nal aḷi (‘good tender love’), which may vāṭiṉum (‘even if it should wither’, a plant metaphor) yet pāṭu peṟum (‘will gain greatness’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take aḷi as the husband’s love that seems to fade during the sulk and then grows in worth; Puliyur Kesikan adds pinnar (‘afterwards’), making the gain explicitly temporal, and Pope renders the sense as feigned anger making drooping affection ‘bloom again’. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the same text; the botanical verb vāṭu (to wilt) is characteristic of the Kural’s Inbam imagery.

tamil:
புலத்தலின் புத்தேள்நாடு உண்டோ நிலத்தொடு
நீரியைந் தன்னார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Pulaththalin puththelnaadu undoa nilaththodu
Neeriyainh thannaar akaththu.
current_meaning: Our hearts are mixed together like water and soil. With such a lover, is there any heaven as sweet as a little sulking?
elementary: When rain soaks into soil, you cannot pull the water back out; the two become one. When two people are that close, even a pretend grumble between them feels happy, because nothing can really pull them apart.
university: Pulattal (‘sulking’, a synonym of ūṭal) is weighed against puttēḷ nāṭu (‘the land of the gods’, heaven), and the rhetorical uṇṭō (‘is there?’) denies that heaven could be sweeter. The simile nilattoṭu nīr iyaintu aṉṉār (‘those who are like water joined with earth’) recalls the famous Kuṟuntokai 40 image of hearts mingled like red earth and rain (cempulap peyalnīr), signalling an inseparable union in which a quarrel holds no danger. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan all read the line as ‘is the gods’ world sweeter than sulking with such a lover?’, while Kalaignar renders puttēḷ nāṭu more freely as ‘a new world’. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi form nīriyain tannār).

tamil:
புல்லி விடாஅப் புலவியுள் தோன்றுமென்
உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை.
transliteration:
Pulli vidaaap pulaviyul thondrumen
Ullam udaikkum padai.
current_meaning: In a sulk that ends with a hug that will not let go, a weapon appears that breaks down my firm mind.
elementary: Imagine deciding to stay cross with your best friend all afternoon, and then they do something so sweet that your crossness just melts. Their kindness is like a magic key that unlocks your grumpy mood. The wife says her husband has that kind of key.
university: The couplet describes a pulavi (‘sulk’) that leads to pulli viṭā (‘embracing and not letting go’, the long vowel in viṭāa marking aḷapeṭai lengthening for metre), within which there arises a paṭai (‘weapon, army’) that uṭaikkum (‘shatters’) eṉ uḷḷam (‘my heart, my firmness’). Commentators identify the weapon with the husband’s tender pleading or caresses, which break the wife’s resolve to keep sulking; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar gloss uḷḷam as uṟuti (‘firmness, determination’). Pope’s ‘a weapon lurks, which quite breaks down my mind’ follows the same line. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தவறிலர் ஆயினும் தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்
அகறலின் ஆங்கொன் றுடைத்து.
transliteration:
Thavarilar aayinum thaamveezhvaar mendroal
Akaralin aangon rudaiththu.
current_meaning: Even when a man has done nothing wrong, being kept for a while from the soft arms of the woman he loves has a joy of its own.
elementary: Waiting for a birthday makes the party feel even better when it comes. A husband who is told ‘not now’ by his wife in a playful sulk, even though he did nothing wrong, finds a funny kind of sweetness in the waiting.
university: Here the voice shifts to the husband, or to a general maxim about men: taviṟilar āyiṉum (‘though they are without fault’), being separated from (akaṟal) the mel tōḷ (‘soft shoulders’, a standard metonymy for the beloved’s embrace) of those whom they love (tām vīḻvār) has āṅku oṉṟu (‘a certain something there’, i.e. a special pleasure). Solomon Pappaiah reads the husband as accepting the role of the guilty one in order to be sulked at, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan simply note that such separation contains a pleasure; Pope renders the thought as estrangement having ‘its own special charms’. The couplet is the same on both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the elided form āṅkoṉṟuṭaittu is split as āṅku oṉṟu uṭaittu.

tamil:
உணலினும் உண்டது அறல்இனிது காமம்
புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Unalinum undadhu aral-inidhu kaamam
Punardhalin oodal inidhu.
current_meaning: Digesting food is sweeter than eating it. In the same way, in love, sulking is sweeter than being together.
elementary: After a big lunch, the cosy, full feeling afterwards can feel even nicer than the eating. The poet says love is similar: the little pause of a pretend quarrel can be sweeter than simply being together.
university: A striking analogy from the body: uṇaliṉum (‘more than eating’) uṇṭatu aṟal (‘the digesting of what has been eaten’, aṟal from aṟu, to be consumed or settle) is iṉitu (‘sweet, pleasant’); likewise in kāmam (love), ūṭal is sweeter than puṇartal (union). Commentators read the parallel as saying that, just as digestion readies one for the next meal, ūṭal renews the appetite of love; Puliyur Kesikan speaks of the pleasure gained ‘by sulking’ exceeding that gained ‘by uniting’. Kalaignar and Pope keep the comparison directly. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh hyphenates aṟal-iṉitu in its transliteration.

tamil:
ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் அதுமன்னும்
கூடலிற் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Oodalil thotravar vendraar adhumannum
Kootalir kaanap padum.
current_meaning: In a lovers' sulk, the one who loses is the one who wins. This becomes clear when they come together again.
elementary: When two friends argue about who gets the swing first, the one who says ‘you go first’ often ends up having the most fun, because the friendship is happy again. In love, the poet says, whoever gives in first is the real winner.
university: The paradox ūṭalil tōṟṟavar veṉṟār (‘those who lost in the sulk have won’) is confirmed, the poet says, in kūṭal (reunion), where atu maṉṉum kāṇappaṭum (‘it will surely be seen’; maṉṉum here an emphatic particle). Kalaignar glosses ūṭal as ‘a sweet war’ (iṉiya pōr), and Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan agree that the truth of the paradox is seen when the couple are reconciled. Commentators differ on who ‘loses’: some take it as the partner who yields to the other’s pleading, others as the one who gives up sulking first; the couplet is often quoted on its own as a maxim for marriage. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊடிப் பெறுகுவம் கொல்லோ நுதல்வெயர்ப்பக்
கூடலில் தோன்றிய உப்பு.
transliteration:
Ootip perukuvam kolloa nudhalveyarppak
Kootalil thoandriya uppu.
current_meaning: By sulking once more, will we win back the sweetness we felt when we came together, when her forehead grew damp with sweat?
elementary: After a really happy day at the beach, you might wish you could have that same day again. The husband in this poem remembers how happy they were after their last make-up, and wonders whether another small quarrel might bring that happiness back.
university: The husband wonders whether, by sulking again (ūṭi), they will once more peṟukuvam (‘obtain’, first person plural, with the doubting particle kollō) the uppu (literally ‘salt’, figuratively ‘savour, relish’) that arose in kūṭal (reunion), when nutal veyarppa (‘the brow grew moist’). Parimelazhagar and the modern glossators take uppu as the relish or sweetness of love, the salt being the zest that makes food tasty; Mu. Varadarasanar renders it as iṉimai (sweetness). Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss (‘ivaḷuṭaṉ’, with her) confirms the traditional reading of this couplet as the husband’s words. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; thirukkural.net keeps the older spelling veyarppa for viyarppa.

tamil:
ஊடுக மன்னோ ஒளியிழை யாமிரப்ப
நீடுக மன்னோ இரா.
transliteration:
Ootuka mannoa oliyizhai yaamirappa
Needuka mannoa iraa.
current_meaning: Let her with the shining jewels sulk a little longer. And let the night grow longer too, so I can keep pleading with her.
elementary: Sometimes making up with a friend is so much fun that you almost wish the game would go on. Here a husband enjoys coaxing his wife out of her playful sulk so much that he wishes the night would stretch out, so he can keep coaxing.
university: Both lines turn on the optative with the particle maṉṉō (‘O, may it be so!’): ūṭuka (‘may she sulk’) and nīṭuka (‘may it lengthen’), framing the hero’s wish. Oḷi iḻai (‘she of bright jewels’) is a standard epithet for the heroine, and yām irappa (‘so that I may beg, plead’) gives the reason for wanting the night (irā) to stretch on. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan agree in reading the couplet as the husband’s wish that her sulk and the night both continue so that he may keep entreating her; Pope renders it ‘That I may still plead on, O night, prolong thy reign!’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம் அதற்கின்பம்
கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Oodudhal kaamaththirku inpam adharkinpam
Kooti muyangap perin.
current_meaning: Sulking is the joy of love, and the joy of sulking is to make up and be held close again.
elementary: A pretend quarrel is a little game that makes love fun, and the best part of the game is the big hug when it is over. With this happy thought, the whole Thirukkural comes to an end.
university: The last couplet of the Kural is built as a chain: ūṭutal kāmattiṟku iṉpam (‘sulking is a delight to love’), ataṟku iṉpam (‘its delight in turn’) is kūṭi muyaṅkap peṟiṉ (‘if one gets to come together and embrace’, muyaṅku meaning to clasp). Solomon Pappaiah adds that the embrace should come aḷavu aṟintu (‘knowing the right measure’), i.e. the sulk must not be stretched too far, a point Parimelazhagar’s tradition also stresses, and Mu. Varadarasanar reads the embrace as the delight that crowns the sulk. Pope ends his translation with ‘The pleasure’s crowned when breast is clasped to breast.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; with this couplet both the kaṟpiyal and the whole 1,330-couplet work conclude, on a note of reconciled love.
